paragraphs.text: I want to set out the precise dates of the captivity that befell the children of Israel, the prophecies contained in the visions of the blessed Daniel, and his upbringing in Babylon from childhood. So I too come forward to bear witness to a holy and righteous man, who became a prophet and a witness of Christ. He not only revealed King Nebuchadnezzar's visions in those days, but also taught youths like himself and brought them forth as faithful witnesses in the world. He lived in the time when the blessed Jeremiah was prophesying, in the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, [who] [?] ... and he was taken along with the rest of the captives and carried off with them to Babylon. While still a young boy, he convicted elders who had grown old in wickedness and given themselves over to evil desire. In this he prefigured the heavenly Judge, who as a youth of twelve was to convict in the temple elders who had become transgressors of the law. The story that has been read took place long ago in Babylon. Its villains were lawless elders serving as judges, who forgot the law of God, became slaves to fleshly desire, and plotted against a chaste woman, attempting unjustly to shed righteous blood. These things had to be fulfilled in them in this way, so that the chosen race of the righteous might be made plain to all, the chastity of the blessed Susanna might be openly displayed, and the righteous and holy prophet Daniel might be shown to the people as a young prophet.

In setting out the proof of these matters, then, we must examine what lies before us with care, so as to persuade our hearers. Let us not leave out what captivities befell the people, of what kind they were, and under which kings they happened. The blessed Josiah had five sons: Jehoahaz; Eliakim, also called Jehoiakim; Johanan; Zedekiah, also called Jeconiah; and Shallum. After his father's death, Jehoahaz was anointed king by the people when he was twenty-three years old. In the third month of his reign Pharaoh Neco came up against him, took him, and led him in chains to Egypt. He imposed on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and ten talents of gold, and in his place he set his brother Eliakim as king over the land, changing his name to Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim reigned eleven years. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against him, took him in chains, and led him to Babylon together with some of the vessels of the house of the Lord in Jerusalem. Because he was a friend of Pharaoh and had been made king by him, he was kept shut up in prison, but in the thirtieth year Evil-merodach king of Babylon brought him out. He shaved his head, made him his counsellor, and he ate at the king's table until the day he died.

After he had been carried away, his son Joakim reigned for three years. Nebuchadnezzar came up against him too and deported him to Babylon along with ten thousand men of the people. In his place he set Jeconiah, his father's brother, changing his name to Zedekiah. He made oaths and a treaty with him and went back to Babylon. After reigning eleven years, Zedekiah revolted from him and gave himself over to Pharaoh king of Egypt. In the twelfth year Nebuchadnezzar came against him with the whole army of the Chaldeans. They threw up a siege wall around the city, encamped against it on every side, and hemmed it in from all directions. So most of the people perished by famine, others fell by the sword, and some were taken captive. The city was burned with fire, and the temple and the wall were torn down. The army of the Chaldeans took all the treasures found in the house of the Lord, and Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, cut up all the vessels of gold and silver and all the bronze and carried them to Babylon. Zedekiah himself, also called Jeconiah, fled by night with seven hundred men. The Chaldean forces pursued him, overtook him at Jericho, and brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah. The king passed judgment on him in anger, because he had broken the oath of the Lord and the covenant he had made with him. He took his sons and slaughtered them before his eyes. Then he put out the eyes of Zedekiah, also called Jeconiah, bound him in iron fetters, and they led him to Babylon. There he ground grain in the mill until the day he died, and when he died they took his body and threw it out behind the wall of Nineveh. In him was fulfilled the prophecy of the prophet Jeremiah, who says: "As I live, says the Lord, even if Jeconiah son of Josiah, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, I would tear you off from there and hand you over to those who seek your life, whom you fear, into the hands of the Chaldeans. I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into a land where you were not born, and there you shall die. But to the land they long for in their souls, they shall never return. Jeconiah has been dishonoured like a useless vessel that no one needs, for he was hurled out and cast into a land he did not know. O land, land, hear the word of the Lord! Write this man down as an outcast, for none of his offspring shall prosper, sitting on the throne of David, as ruler any longer in Judah."

So when the whole people had been deported, the city laid waste, and the sanctuary torn down, fulfilling the word that the Lord spoke through the mouth of the prophet Jeremiah, that the sanctuary would lie desolate for seventy years, we find the blessed Daniel prophesying in Babylon and coming to Susanna's defence.

For the scripture says: "There was a man living in Babylon whose name was Joakim. He took a wife named Susanna, the daughter of Hilkiah, a very beautiful woman who feared the Lord. Her parents were righteous and had taught their daughter according to the law of Moses." This story took place later, but it was written down first in the book. The scribes were in the habit of putting many things in the scriptures out of order, later events before earlier ones. In the prophets too we find some visions that were seen first and fulfilled at the end, and others told at the end that were seen first. This happened by the design of the Spirit, so that the devil might not understand what the prophets spoke in parables, and so ensnare man a second time and kill him again.

The book begins like this: "In the third year of the reign of Joakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. And the Lord gave Joakim king of Judah into his hand, together with some of the vessels of the house of God, and he carried them to the land of Shinar, to the house of his god." Scripture relates this in order to point to the captivity of the people that took place when Joakim, son of Eliakim (also called Jehoiakim), was deported, and with him the three youths, who were taken together with Daniel. This Joakim was Susanna's husband.

The scripture says: "The king told Ashpenaz, his chief eunuch, to bring in some of the sons of the captivity of Israel, from the royal family and from the nobles: young men without blemish, handsome in appearance, skilled in all wisdom, endowed with knowledge, understanding and discernment, and able to serve in the king's palace, and to teach them the letters and language of the Chaldeans. The king assigned them a daily portion from the king's table and from the wine he drank, and ordered that they be brought up for three years, and after that stand before the king. Among them, from the sons of Judah, were Daniel and Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah." Those who love learning should not read this hastily, but should fix their minds on what lies before them. The divine scriptures proclaim nothing idle to us: they speak for our own instruction, for the blessing of these prophets, and as proof of all that they spoke. For when Hezekiah king of Judah fell sick to the point of death, the prophet Isaiah came to him and said to him: "Give your instructions concerning your sons and your daughters and your father's house, for you are dying and will not live." Grieved at these words, Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying: "Lord, remember me, how I have walked before you in truth and faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is pleasing in your sight." And Hezekiah wept bitterly. After this Isaiah was sent to him a second time and said to him: "Thus says the Lord, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. See, I am adding fifteen years of life to your days, and I will deliver you from the hand of the king of Assyria. And this shall be the sign to you from the Lord that the Lord will do this thing that he has spoken: see, I will turn back the shadow on the steps of your father's house, which the sun has gone down, the ten steps which the shadow has gone down," so that that day became thirty-two hours long. The sun had run its course and reached the tenth hour, and the shadow had gone down the ten steps of the temple house. Then, at the word of the Lord, the sun turned back again the ten steps, and that made twenty hours. Then the sun once more ran its own course in its proper order and went on to its setting, and so there were thirty-two hours.

But perhaps someone will say that this is impossible. O man, what is impossible for God? Did he not in the beginning create the whole creation out of nothing, and set in it the heavenly bodies to give light by day and by night? Are not all things subject to him and his servants, and do they not tremble as they obey his voice? What is impossible with men, then, is possible with God. On this point we also have another testimony that is easy to accept. When Joshua son of Nun was fighting the Amorites, the sun had already sunk toward its setting while the battle was at its height. The blessed Joshua feared that once night fell the foreigners would escape, and he cried out: "Let the sun stand still over Gibeon, and the moon over the valley of Aijalon, until I have defeated this people." And the sun and the moon stood still where they were; the sun did not go on toward its setting until the end of a whole day, so that that day became twenty-four hours long. That is why the scripture bore witness, saying: "There has never been a day like this, when God listened to a man." He who in the beginning fixed the bounds of the heavenly bodies and appointed them their ever-moving courses by his own authority, how could he not also be able to shift them, turn them and change them whenever he wishes? In the time of Joshua the sun stood still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Aijalon for a whole day. In the time of Hezekiah the moon too turned back along with the sun, so that the two bodies would not collide by moving against each other out of order. But at the Lord's passion, not only the heavenly bodies but the day itself and the whole world were shaken.

In the days of Hezekiah, Merodach the Chaldean, king of Babylonia, was likewise astonished at what had happened, for he practised the art of astrology and measured the courses of the heavenly bodies precisely. When he learned the cause, he sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah. The magi who came from the East did the same: when the Lord was born in Bethlehem and the star appeared in the sky as had been prophesied, the magi, amazed at the sign that had appeared, came to Jerusalem saying, "Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him." In the same way the Chaldeans of that time, finding that the sun had not kept its usual course, honoured Hezekiah with gifts and letters as a God-fearing and righteous man, marvelling at the sign God had given him. Hezekiah rejoiced at this and showed them all the treasures in the house of the Lord, and then all his wealth and his glory. Afterwards the prophet Isaiah said, "Who are these men, and where have they come to you from?" Hezekiah answered, "They have come to me from a distant land, from the land of Babylon." Isaiah said to him, "What did they see in your house?" Hezekiah said, "They saw everything in my house; there is nothing I did not show them, even what is in my treasuries." And Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the Lord Almighty, the Lord of Hosts. See, days are coming, says the Lord, when everything in your house, and all that your fathers have stored up until this day, will be carried off and will come to Babylon, and they will leave nothing behind, says the Lord. And some of your children [who will come from you], whom you have fathered, they will take away, and they will be eunuchs in the king's palace."

So, in order that what the Lord had said might be fulfilled and the prophet be shown to speak the truth, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came and took all the treasures found in the house of the Lord and led the people into captivity. He took for himself as servants the king's sons and the most nobly born of the nobles. Among those chosen were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. Scripture passes over their lineage in silence, but it tells of their piety and faithfulness and of what they did there. Having possessed the fear of God from childhood, they refused to partake of the king's table or to drink of the wine he drank, so as not to defile their pure mouths. O blessed youths, who kept the covenant of their fathers and did not transgress the law given through Moses, but feared the God proclaimed through him! Though they were captives in a foreign land, they were not seduced by fancy foods, nor enslaved by the wine of pleasure, nor enticed by royal glory. Carried off as they were, they kept their mouths holy and pure, so that a pure word, coming from a pure mouth, might hymn the heavenly Father through it, as it is written: "If you bring forth what is precious from what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth." Do you understand, O man, what is being said? The Father's mouth brought forth from itself a precious Word, so that the Word might be shown to be born a second time from saints: he always begets the saints, and he himself is in turn begotten by saints.

The scripture says: "Daniel resolved in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king's table or with the wine he drank, and he asked the chief eunuch to give them vegetables," in order to show that man shall not live by bread alone. "And God brought Daniel into favour and compassion before the chief eunuch. The chief eunuch said to him: 'I am afraid of my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink. What if he should see your faces looking gloomier than those of the youths of your own age? You would endanger my head with the king.'" What Melgad said was reasonable enough. Not knowing what was being arranged through them, he was afraid that their faces would look gloomier than those of the youths who ate from the king's table, and that he would be found responsible and handed over to death. They wanted to prove to him that it is not earthly food that gives people beauty and strength, but the grace of God bestowed through the Word, and so they said to him: "Test your servants for ten days. Let us be given vegetables to eat and water to drink. Then compare our appearance with the appearance of the youths who eat from the king's table, and deal with us according to what you see." Do you see the youths' unwavering faith and their unshakeable fear of God? They asked for a space of ten days, to show by this that people cannot obtain grace from God in any other way than by believing in the Word proclaimed through Jesus.

The scripture says: "The chief eunuch listened to them and tested them for ten days. At the end of the ten days their appearance was seen to be better, and they were sturdier in body than the youths who ate from the king's table." Fed only on bread and water, but adorned with heavenly wisdom, they found more favour than all the youths of their age. "For God gave them understanding and insight in all learning and wisdom, and Daniel had understanding in every vision and dream. At the end of the days the chief eunuch brought them in before the king, and the king spoke with them, and among them all none was found like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah." So the Word brought these youths forth, endowed with all wisdom, to be shown as faithful witnesses in Babylon, so that through them the objects of Babylonian worship might be put to shame, Nebuchadnezzar might be defeated by three youths, the fire in the furnace might be put to flight through their faith, the blessed Susanna might be rescued from death, and the vain lust of the lawless elders might be exposed. These four youths, cared for by God and holding the fear of God in their hearts, won these victories in the city of Babylon. Come forward, then, blessed Daniel, you who came to the defence of the blessed Susanna, so that you may also show us the things to come.

For the scripture says: "There was a man living in Babylon whose name was Joakim. He took a wife named Susanna, the daughter of Hilkiah, a very beautiful woman who feared the Lord." This is the man we spoke of earlier, who, while living as an exile in Babylon, took Susanna as his wife. She was the daughter of Hilkiah the priest, who found the book of the law in the house of the Lord when King Josiah ordered him to cleanse the Holy of Holies. Her brother was the prophet Jeremiah, who, after the people had been carried captive to Babylon, was taken to Egypt with those who were left. He lived at Tahpanhes and, while prophesying there, was stoned to death by them. These, then, were of priestly stock, from the tribe of Levi, and they intermarried with the tribe of Judah. In this way, through the coming together of the two righteous tribes, the righteous seed of Christ according to the flesh would be made plain, and he who was born of them in Bethlehem would be shown to be King and Priest of God. For Matthew, wanting to trace Christ's lineage according to the flesh down to Joseph pure and unblemished, came to Josiah, passed over his five sons, and named Jeconiah, who was born in Babylon of Susanna, moving from righteous seed to righteous seed. For he says: "Josiah fathered Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the deportation to Babylon." How can this be proved? Josiah reigned thirty-one years in the land of Judah and died there. How, then, could he father Jeconiah in Babylon when he had died back there? From this we must understand that Matthew included in the genealogy the Jeconiah born of Joakim and Susanna, counting him as the son of Eliakim, also called Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah. Matthew could not have traced the genealogy through the Jeconiah whom the Holy Spirit had declared an outcast, as some mistakenly suppose. That man was blinded and taken to Babylon, where he was shut up in chains in the mill and died childless. So it is not for nothing that the scripture teaches us: "There was a man living in Babylon whose name was Joakim. He took a wife named Susanna, the daughter of Hilkiah, a very beautiful woman who feared the Lord." Of her, then, Jeconiah was born; Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel, and Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel went up to Jerusalem together with Ezra the scribe and Jeshua son of Jozadak, at the command of Cyrus the Persian. Thus the lineage of the fathers remained pure until the birth of Jesus Christ.

"Her parents," it says, "were righteous and had taught their daughter according to the law of Moses." The tree is easily known from the fruit it puts forth. These devout men, zealous for the law, brought into the world children worthy of God: one became a prophet and a witness of Christ, and the other was found chaste and faithful in Babylon, and her modesty and chastity showed the blessed Daniel to be a prophet. "Joakim," it says, "was very rich and had a garden next to his house, and the Jews used to gather at his house, because he was the most honoured of them all. That year two elders from the people were appointed judges. Of them the Master said, 'Lawlessness came forth from Babylon, from elders who were judges, who seemed to govern the people.' These men were constantly at Joakim's house, and all who had lawsuits came to them there." We must look into the reason for this. How could these people, who were captives and had become subject to the Babylonians, gather together as if they were free? Here we must understand that after deporting them, Nebuchadnezzar treated them kindly and allowed them to meet together and do everything according to the law. Having been given this authority, they appointed two rulers of the people, who seemed to govern the people. These men were constantly at Joakim's house, because he was more honoured and wealthier than all the rest, being of royal descent.

He had a garden next to his house. “And it came to pass that when the people went away at midday, Susanna would go in and walk in her husband’s garden. And the two elders watched her every day, and they came to desire her.” The rulers of the Jews now want to cut these things out of the book. They claim that these things did not happen in Babylon, because they are ashamed of what the elders did at that time, and they do not understand the plan of the Spirit. The divine Scriptures show everything impartially and openly. They show not only the righteous deeds of men, by which they were justified, but also the terrible things some have done, in which these [?] become entangled and perish. The purpose is that those who fear God may imitate the righteous and so walk in righteousness, while those who do the opposite may keep before their eyes the punishment that awaits them from God. For what the elders did to Susanna back then is being done in the same way now by the rulers of the present Babylon. Susanna was a prefiguring type of the Church, and Joakim her husband a type of Christ. The garden was the calling of the saints, who are planted in the Church like fruit-bearing trees. Babylon is the world. The two elders are presented as a type of the two peoples who plot against the Church, one from the circumcision and one from the Gentiles. When it says that they “were appointed rulers of the people and judges,” it means that in this age they hold power and rule, and they judge the righteous unjustly.

The text says that they “eagerly watched Susanna every day” as she walked in the garden. This means that to this day both the Gentiles and the Jews of the circumcision watch closely and pry into what is done in the Church, because they want to bring false testimony against us. As the apostle says: “Because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy on the freedom that we have in Christ Jesus.” In the same way, it says, those elders “eagerly watched every day to see her, and they perverted their own minds and turned away their eyes so as not to look to heaven or remember just judgments.” For how can those who have become plotters against the Church and its corrupters judge justly, or look up to heaven with a pure heart, when they are enslaved to the ruler of this age? “And both were stricken with passion for her, but they did not tell each other of their pain, because they were ashamed to disclose their desire to lie with her.” What is said here can indeed be truly understood. The two peoples, stung by Satan who works in them, are always plotting to stir up persecutions and afflictions against the Church, striving to destroy her, even though they do not agree among themselves. “And one said to the other, ‘Let us go home, for it is time for lunch.’ And they went out and parted from each other. Then they turned back and came to the same place.” That they parted from each other at lunchtime and turned back to the same place means that the Jews do not agree with the Gentiles about earthly foods, but they join them and share with them at the public shows and in every worldly affair. So the Scripture says: “And when they questioned each other about the reason, they confessed their desire.” They were prophesying about themselves, that they would be examined by angels and would have to give account to God for every sin they had committed. As Solomon says: “Examination will destroy the ungodly.” For these men are caught when their wickedness is examined.

“And it came to pass, while they were watching for a suitable day, that she went in one day, as on the day before and the day before that, with only two maids, and she wished to bathe in the garden, for it was hot.” So it came to pass “while they were watching for a suitable day.” What suitable day does the Scripture mean, if not the day of the Pasch? On that day the bath is prepared in the garden for those who are burning with heat, and the Church, washed like Susanna, is presented to God as a pure bride. The Scripture says that “she went in as on the day before and the day before that, with only two maids, and she wished to bathe in the garden.” This shows that whenever the Church wishes to receive the spiritual bath, as is her custom, two maidservants must accompany her. For the Church receives the bath through faith in Christ and through love toward God, confessing [?]. And the two maidservants who accompany her, faith and love, prepare the oil and the ointments for those who are being washed. What were the ointments, if not the commandments of the Word? And what is the oil, if not the power of the Holy Spirit? With these, as with perfume, believers are anointed after the bath. These things were prefigured long ago in the blessed Susanna for our sake. So now we who believe in God should not regard what is done in the Church today as something strange. Instead we should believe that these things were prefigured long ago through the patriarchs. As the apostle also says: “These things happened to them as types, and they were written down for our instruction, on whom the ends of the ages have come.”

Those who love learning can see very clearly that the garden planted by God in Eden became a type and image of the Church. From earthly things we must glimpse heavenly things as in a mirror. From things that are types we must recognize spiritual things, and from temporary things we must look forward to eternal ones. So God commanded Moses to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain. What had he seen, if not images of heavenly glories and forms? In imitation of these he built the bodily tabernacle out of wood that does not rot. In this way earthly things were made plain to those who think in a fleshly way, while the heavenly things to come were made plain to the spiritual. Eden means a place of delight, that is, a garden. It was planted toward the east and adorned with beautiful trees and every kind of fruit. So we may understand that the assembly of the righteous is a holy place in which the Church was planted. A bare place cannot be called a church, nor can a house built of stone and clay. Nor can a man by himself be called a church, for a house falls down and a man dies. What, then, is the Church? It is the assembly of saints who live in the truth. The harmony of the saints and their journey together become the Church, a spiritual house of God planted on Christ as in the east. In it, those who enter see trees of many kinds in full bloom: the generation of the fathers set apart from the beginning; the works of the prophets, which were fulfilled after the Law; the choir of apostles, made wise through the Word; all the martyrs, saved through the blood of Christ; the company of virgins, sanctified through water; the choir of teachers; and the order of bishops, priests and Levites. All these, adorned with every kind of variety, flourish in the Church and cannot decay. We share in their fruits and rejoice, eating the spiritual and heavenly food that comes from them. For the blessed patriarchs themselves served God’s oracles to us like flourishing trees planted in a garden, always carrying their fruit with them. They did this so that to this day we might know Christ, the sweet fruit that came forth from them, given to us as the fruit of life. In this Eden a river of ever-flowing waters streams out, and four rivers go out from it and water all the land of men. The same is seen in the Church. Christ is the river, and through the fourfold saving Gospel he guards all things and is present to all. He waters and gives drink to all who believe in him, as the prophet says: “Rivers will flow from his belly.” In the garden there was shown a tree of knowledge and a tree of life. In the same way, the Law and the Word are now shown in the Church like two trees planted there. For through the Law comes knowledge of sin, while through the Word life and forgiveness of trespasses are given. In that time Adam disobeyed God and tasted from the tree of knowledge, and he was cast out of the garden. He had been taken from the earth, and he returned to the earth again. In the same way, anyone who has believed but has not kept the commandments is stripped of the Holy Spirit and cast out of the Church. No longer receiving [?], he becomes earth and must return to his old self.

When the Scripture says, “Susanna would go in and walk in her husband’s garden,” it means that all kings and people of high rank plant gardens for their own delight in cities and in the countryside, as Joakim did in Babylon. For he had a garden next to his house, and Susanna would go in and walk there. She devoted herself to prayer and sang hymns and songs to God. She sent out the two maids to bring what she had ordered, so that she could bathe. The maids shut the doors of the garden and went out by the side door. In this they foretold what was to come: whoever wishes to share in the water in the garden must renounce the wide doors and enter through the narrow and hard way. “And they did not see the elders, because they were hidden.” Just as the devil once hid in the serpent in the garden, so now he hid in the elders and stirred up his own lust, so that he might corrupt Eve a second time.

“And it came to pass, when the maids had gone out, that the two elders got up and ran to her and said, ‘Look, the doors of the garden are shut, and no one sees us, and we desire you. So consent to us and lie with us. If you refuse, we will testify against you that a young man was with you, and that this is why you sent your maids away.’” O lawless rulers and leaders filled with the devil’s working! Is this what Moses handed down to you? Is this how you read the Law and teach others? You who say, “Do not commit adultery,” do you commit adultery yourselves? You who preach, “Do not kill,” do you kill yourselves? You who say, “Do not covet,” do you want to corrupt your neighbor’s wife yourselves? Tell me, rulers of Israel: does God, who made all things, not see this? Do the day and the sun not see what you are doing? Will the earth that you defile not cry out? Why, you lawless men, do you try to win over a chaste and innocent soul with lying words, to satisfy your own lust? The same thing happened to Naboth the Israelite. He would not agree to give his vineyard to Ahab to be made into a vegetable garden, and for this the righteous man was falsely accused and unjustly put to death. These have been your terrible crimes from the beginning, because of the deceiver who has lurked in you from the beginning. There was indeed a young man with her, a young man from heaven, not to lie with her but to stand by her.

When the blessed Susanna heard these words, she was pierced to the heart and shielded her body, because she did not want to be defiled by lawless elders. What happened to Susanna can truly be understood, for you will find it being fulfilled now in the Church as well. Whenever the two peoples agree to corrupt the souls of the saints, they watch for a suitable day. They burst into the house of God while everyone there is praying and singing hymns to God. They seize some and drag them off and hold them, saying: “Come, consent to us and worship our gods. If you refuse, we will testify against you.” When these refuse, they bring them before the governors and accuse them of acting against Caesar’s decree, and they are condemned to death.

Then Susanna groaned and said: “I am hemmed in on every side. If I do this, it is death for me. If I do not, I will not escape your hands. But I choose not to do it and to fall into your hands rather than to sin before the Lord.” See the words of a chaste woman devoted to God! “I am hemmed in,” she says, “on every side.” For the Church is afflicted and hemmed in not only by Jews but also by Gentiles and by those falsely called Christians. They always see her chastity and steadfastness and try to corrupt her by force. “If I do this,” she says, “it is death for me.” For to disobey God and obey men brings about death and eternal punishment. “If I do not, I will not escape your hands.” This too she said truly. Those who are brought to trial for the name of Christ die to God and live to the world if they do what men command. If they refuse, they do not escape the hands of the judges, but are condemned by those same judges and die. For it is better for us to refuse and fall into their hands than to sin before the Lord. It is far better to die unjustly at the hands of men so that we may live with God, than to agree with them and be released by them, only to fall into the hands of God. For this is why our Lord Jesus Christ lived and died and rose again: to be Lord of both the living and the dead.

The blessed Susanna taught us these things long ago, prefiguring in herself the mysteries of the Church in every respect. Her faithfulness, her piety and the chastity of her body are proclaimed to this day throughout the whole earth. So I urge all of you who read this Scripture, women and virgins, small and great: keep God’s judgment before your eyes, take her as an example, and imitate her. Then, like Susanna, you will be able to be vindicated by God and rescued from the second death by the Word who lived in Daniel. You men, seek the dignity of Joseph, and you women, the purity and faithfulness of Susanna. Give no occasion for slander against yourselves, so that you do not make what the elders said look true. For many liars and deceivers have crept in and are leading astray the innocent souls of the saints. Some corrupt women with persuasive words and draw them into their own lusts. Others overturn men with heretical words, so that they may carry out their own will. Foreseeing what would happen, the apostle said: “I am afraid that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may be corrupted and led away from the knowledge of Christ.” Wake up, all you saints, I beg you! Love the truth and recognize the purity of Susanna. She was not enslaved to the flesh and the desire for pleasure, nor was she swept away by the rank of the elders. She feared God with her whole heart and chose temporary death so that she might escape the second death, the death of fire.

While this was happening, the Scripture says: “And Susanna cried out with a loud voice, and the two elders also cried out against her.” To whom did Susanna cry out, if not to God? As Isaiah also says: “Then you will cry out, and God will hear you; while you are still speaking he will say, ‘Here I am.’” “And the two elders also cried out against her.” For the lawless never stop crying out against us and saying, “Away with such a one from the earth! It is not fit that they should live.” “And one of them ran and opened the doors of the garden.” He was pointing to the wide and spacious road by which those who obey such men perish. The maids, on the other hand, showed us the narrow side door, through which they themselves went out.

“And the servants heard Susanna’s voice and came in.” But the elders did the opposite and opened the wide doors, contriving some pretext for putting her to death. “When the elders had told their story, the servants were deeply ashamed, for nothing evil had ever been said about Susanna.” Beloved, see how living chastely from childhood brings people praise until death! The same thing happened to Susanna. She had studied the law of Moses carefully from infancy and lived with dignity and chastity, and so she made the accusation the elders spoke against her impossible to believe. So too every believing man or woman who keeps the faith they received and fears God will not sin. But anyone who is called a believer and does the works of an unbeliever will receive a double judgment from God, even if he seems to escape notice now in this world.

“And it came to pass on the next day, when the people gathered at the house of her husband Joakim, that the two elders came too, full of their lawless scheme against Susanna to put her to death. And they said before the people, ‘Send for Susanna the daughter of Hilkiah, the wife of Joakim.’ So they sent for her, and she came with her parents, her children and all her relatives.” This can be seen now as well. Whenever one of the saints is arrested and brought into court, everyone runs together there to see what will happen to him. “Now Susanna was very delicate and beautiful to look at.” She was clothed with beauty, but not with the beauty of a harlot’s body, such as Jezebel wore, nor with a face painted in many colors. Hers was the beauty of faith, chastity and holiness. “And the lawless men ordered her to be unveiled, for she was veiled, so that they might feast their eyes on her beauty.” Let us consider, beloved, whose evil working this is. The apostle said, “A woman ought to have a covering on her head because of the angels.” These men did the opposite. They ordered her to be unveiled before the people, and they were not ashamed of it. “And they stood up in the midst of the people and laid their hands on her head.” They did this so that by touching her they might satisfy their lust to the full. “But she wept and looked up to heaven, for her heart trusted in the Lord.” Through her tears she drew down the Word from heaven, the one who was to raise the dead Lazarus through tears.

“And the elders said: ‘While we were walking alone in the garden, this woman came in with two maids. She shut the doors of the garden and dismissed the maids. Then a young man who had been hiding came to her and lay with her. We were in a corner of the garden, and when we saw this lawless deed, we ran to them. We saw them lying together, but we could not hold him, because he was stronger than we were, and he opened the doors and leaped out. We seized this woman and asked her who the young man was, but she would not tell us. To these things we testify.’ And they believed them, since they were elders of the people and judges, and they condemned her to death.” So we must stand firm in every matter. We must not listen to lying words, nor be easily carried away by the rank of rulers and believe them, since we know that we must give account to God. Instead, we must hold to the truth, seek the exact meaning of the faith, and be pleasing to God. For long ago the children of Israel were easily persuaded by their rulers and did not examine the truth, and so they became guilty of murder by unjustly condemning Susanna. But she called on the Avenger from heaven and cried out, saying: “Eternal God, who know what is hidden, who know all things before they come to be, you know that they have borne false witness against me. And look, I am dying, though I have done none of the wicked things these men have charged against me.” “And God heard her voice.” For God listens to all who call on him from a pure heart, but he turns his face away from those who call on him with deceit and hypocrisy.

“And as she was being led away to die,” it says, “God roused the Holy Spirit in a young boy named Daniel, and he cried out with a loud voice, ‘I am innocent of this woman’s blood.’” What is it that happened here, beloved? Let us pay attention. Why did this visitation from the Lord not come before she was condemned, but only as she was being led away to be put to death? So that the majesty and power of God might be shown. How so? When God wishes to rescue one of his servants, he can rescue and save him whenever and however he wishes. But when he wishes to take him to himself, he lets him perish, so that after he has endured the torments he may crown him as a noble athlete and glorify him. When Susanna had prayed and been heard, an angel of the Lord was sent out to become her avenger and helper, to destroy those who were plotting against her. The blessed Daniel saw him coming, for he was a prophet and had the Spirit of God, and he cried out, “I am innocent of this woman’s blood.” He said this so that he too would not become guilty of murder, as Pilate did in the case of Christ. Pilate washed his hands with water, saying, “I am innocent of this man’s blood.”

But perhaps someone will say that this is asserted without warrant in Scripture, and that it cannot be known whether Daniel cried out “I am innocent of this woman’s blood” because he had seen the angel. If you wait a little, my friend, Daniel himself will teach you. For when the people heard his voice and were amazed, he answered them: “Are you such fools, children of Israel? Have you condemned a daughter of Israel without examining the case or learning the plain truth? Now go back to the place of judgment, for these men have borne false witness against her.” And the people hurried back. But the lawless elders mocked Daniel and scorned him as a mere boy, not perceiving the power of the Word within him, and they spoke up, saying: “Come, sit among us and tell us, since God has given you the standing of an elder.” He said: “Separate them far from each other, and I will examine them.” When they had been separated one from the other, he called one of them and said to him: “You who have grown old in wicked days, now your sins have come home, the sins you committed in the past, giving unjust judgments, condemning the innocent and acquitting the guilty, though the Lord says, ‘You shall not put to death the innocent and the righteous.’ Now then, if you really saw this woman, tell me: under what tree did you see them keeping company with each other?” He said: “Under a mastic tree.” And Daniel said: “Truly you have lied against your own head, for the angel of God has already gone out, having received the sentence from God to cut you in two.” So Daniel has resolved the question. For to say, “The angel of God has already gone out, having received the sentence from God to cut you in two,” shows that when Susanna prayed to God and was heard, an angel was then sent out to help her. The same thing happened in the case of Tobit and Sarah: when they prayed, in that very hour and on that very day the petition of both was heard, and the angel Raphael was sent to heal the two of them. So then, the Scripture foretold this through the prophet Amos, saying to the house of Israel: “Will the Lord God do anything unless he first reveals it to his servants the prophets?” A vision came to Daniel, and the Holy Spirit was stirred up in him, so that, as he conducted the examination, the angel might deal with these men as wicked false witnesses.

But since we explained earlier, in the introduction, that the two elders are to be taken as a figure of the two peoples, the one from the circumcision and the one from the Gentiles, who are always plotting against the Church, let us look at the words of Daniel himself and learn that Scripture deceives us in nothing. When he said to the first, “You who have grown old in wicked days, now your sins have come home, the sins you committed in the past, giving unjust judgments, condemning the innocent and acquitting the guilty, though the Lord says, ‘You shall not put to death the innocent and the righteous,’” he was speaking to him as to one learned in the Law and as one who loved the Law. But to the other he did not speak in this way; instead he said to him, “Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah.” By calling him a Canaanite he showed that he was, as it were, a Gentile, and he spoke to him as to an uncircumcised man: “So desire has deceived you, and beauty has perverted your heart? This is how you have been treating the daughters of Israel, and they, out of fear, consorted with you; but a daughter of Judah would not submit to your wickedness. Now then, if you really saw this woman, tell me: under what tree did you see them keeping company with each other?” He said: “Under an evergreen oak.” And Daniel said: “Truly you too have lied against your own head, for the angel of God is about to saw you in two, so as to destroy you both.”

So then, that the dignity of the holy Scriptures may be preserved in all things, and the pure mouth of the blessed prophets be shown to be pure, let us compare word with word and set expression beside expression. When the elders of that time wanted to beguile their own lust with foul words and said shamelessly, “We saw them lying together,” blessed Daniel gave a decent form to what they had spoken so basely and so foully, saying to them, “Under what tree did you see them keeping company with each other?” For keeping company is one notion, and sexual intercourse quite another.

When this had happened, it says, the whole assembly cried out with a loud voice and gave praise to God, because Daniel had convicted them out of their own mouths of bearing false witness. What, then, shall we say? The proof lay in this: that one said a mastic tree and the other an evergreen oak. For what might they have wanted to say? “While we were trying to get hold of the young man, we did not see clearly what kind of tree it was.” But since in all things the divine Scripture makes us wise, guiding us toward the truth, we must understand here that they were compelled by the Spirit to name trees of a kind that had not been planted in the garden, so that they might accuse themselves out of their own mouths. For if they had named one of the trees planted there, they might perhaps have persuaded the people by that word. As it was, however, this was not so: they declared things that did not exist. For when Daniel had exposed through his words the thoughts of their hearts, had spoken out the dreadful lust they still had in their eyes, and had brought to light the secret offenses they had committed from the beginning against the daughters of Israel, they, being convicted by the Holy Spirit and darkened in mind, named trees foreign to the place, so that through their own word they might trip themselves up.

Therefore, when all the people and all her relatives heard this, they cried out, saying: “They have lied! For neither a mastic tree nor an evergreen oak is planted in the garden.” After this the whole assembly rose and gave praise to God, who saves those who hope in him. And they rose up against the two elders and did to them what they had wickedly intended to do to their neighbor, and they put them to death, because Daniel had convicted them out of their own mouths of bearing false witness, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will himself fall into it.” And innocent blood was saved that day. Hilkiah and his wife praised God for their daughter, together with Joakim her husband and all their relatives, because nothing shameful had been found in her. And from that day onward Daniel became great in the sight of the people.

We ought, then, to be attentive in all things, beloved, fearing lest anyone, caught in some transgression, should by his own doing become guilty against his own soul, knowing that God is the avenger of all things; for he is himself all eye, and nothing done in the world escapes him. Therefore, always keeping watch in your hearts and living soberly, imitate Susanna: take your delight in the garden, enjoy the ever-flowing water, wash away all filth, and be sanctified with heavenly oil, so that you may present a pure body to God, kindle your lamps, and wait for the bridegroom, so that when he knocks you may receive him and sing praise to God through Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

"In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed a dream, and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him. And the king commanded that the enchanters, the magicians, the sorcerers and the Chaldeans be called to tell the king his dreams; and they came and stood before the king. And the king said to them: I have dreamed a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know the dream. And the Chaldeans spoke to the king in Aramaic: O king, live for ever! Tell the dream to your servants, and we will declare the interpretation. The king answered the Chaldeans: The matter has gone from me. If, then, you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you will be destroyed and your houses will be plundered; but if you make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you will receive from me gifts and rewards and great honour. Only declare to me the dream and its interpretation."

Now the dream that the king had seen was not earthly, so that it could be interpreted by the wise men of the world; it was heavenly, and it was to be fulfilled in its own appointed times according to the counsel and providence of God. That is why it was hidden from people who set their minds on earthly things, so that the heavenly mysteries might be revealed to those who seek heavenly things. The same thing happened in Egypt in the time of Pharaoh. When he had seen his dreams, he related them to all the interpreters of Egypt, and there was no one who could explain them to Pharaoh; but when blessed Joseph was present, what others could not understand was made plain at the right moment. And so the king, in amazement, answered his servants: "Can we find such a man as this, in whom is the Spirit of God?" By this Scripture indicates that no one will be able to explain the heavenly mysteries unless he interprets them as one who shares in the Holy Spirit. So too in Babylon the vision was hidden from the king, so that Daniel, chosen by God, might be shown to be a prophet. For when things hidden from some are made plain by another, this necessarily proves that the one who declares them is a prophet.

So that the Chaldeans might not contrive some way of deceiving the king with lying words, Nebuchadnezzar, deeply troubled, said to them: "I know for certain that you are trying to gain time, because you see that the matter has gone from me. If, then, you do not tell me the dream, I know that you have agreed to speak a false and corrupt word before me until the time has passed." The Chaldeans answered the king, saying: "There is no man on earth who will be able to make known the king's matter, since no great king or ruler asks such a thing of any enchanter, magician, sorcerer or Chaldean. For the thing that the king asks is hard, and there is no one else who will declare it before the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with any flesh." When this had been said, the king was enraged and ordered all the wise men of Babylon to be put to death. And the decree went out, and the wise men were being killed.

Since, then, they had declared it impossible for any human being to tell what the king was asking, God showed them that what is impossible with human beings is possible with God. For Arioch the chief cook was about to put Daniel and his three friends to death—he had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon. Scripture calls him "chief cook," meaning the commander of the knife: for just as a cook slaughters all animals and cooks them, in the same way the rulers of this world slaughter human beings, cooking them like brute beasts. Daniel came up and said: "Why has this shameless decree gone out from the king's presence?" For he wanted to learn from him the reason why the Babylonians were being put to death. And Arioch made the matter known to Daniel. When he had heard it, Daniel asked him to give him time, so that he might make the interpretation known to the king.

Then Daniel went into his house and made the matter known to Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. And they sought mercy from the God of heaven, so that they might not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night. And Daniel blessed the God of heaven, saying: "May the name of the Lord be blessed from everlasting to everlasting, for wisdom and understanding and might are his. He changes times and seasons; he sets up kings and removes them; he gives wisdom to the wise and prudence to those who have understanding. He reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light is with him. To you, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, for you have given me wisdom and power, and have made known to me what we asked of you; you have made known to me the king's matter." We ought therefore to recognize the compassion of God: how quickly he reveals and makes things plain to those who are worthy and fear him, fulfilling their prayers and requests, as the prophet says: "Who is wise, and will understand these things? And who is discerning, and will know them?"

When this had happened, Daniel rose and went to Arioch and said to him: "Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon; bring me in before the king, and I will tell the king the dream and its interpretation." When he heard this, he brought Daniel in with haste and said: "I have found a man among the exiles from Judah who will declare the interpretation to the king." The king, astonished, said to Daniel: "Can you tell me the dream that I saw and its interpretation?" And Daniel said: "The mystery that the king asks about is not something that magicians, enchanters or diviners can declare to the king; but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and he has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what must come to pass in the last days." See how by these words he rescues the Chaldeans from the danger of being put to death, and teaches the king not to seek from earthly men the heavenly mysteries, which were to be accomplished by God in their own times. And so, directing the king's mind toward God, he said: "There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries," from whom a person must receive them by asking with entreaties and prayers. Accordingly he himself, being humble-minded and making himself small, and not boasting that he had been found wiser than all the Babylonians, said: "And as for me, this mystery was not revealed to me because of any wisdom in me beyond all who dwell on the earth, but so that the interpretation might be made known to the king, and that you might know the thoughts of your heart." For the king, having conquered Egypt, taken possession of the land of Judea and deported its people, was pondering as he lay on his bed what would come to pass after these things. And he who knows the secrets of all and searches the thoughts of the heart revealed to him through the image the things that were to be, but hid the vision from him, so that God's counsels could not be interpreted by the wise men of Babylon, but what was hidden from all might be made plain by blessed Daniel, as a prophet of God.

So he says: "You, O king, were watching, and behold, a single image. That image was great, and its appearance was terrifying. It was an image whose head was of fine gold, its hands and chest and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, its legs of iron, its feet partly of iron and partly of clay. You watched until a stone was cut out without hands, and it struck the image on its feet of iron and clay and crushed them completely. Then the clay, the iron, the bronze, the silver and the gold were crushed all at once, and became like chaff from the summer threshing floor; and the force of the wind carried them away, and no place was found for them. And the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth. This is the dream, and we will tell its interpretation before the king. You, O king, are king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given a kingdom strong and mighty and honoured in every place where the children of men dwell; and he has given into your hand the beasts of the field and the birds of the air, and made you lord over them all. You are the head of gold. After you another kingdom will arise, inferior to you; and a third kingdom, which is the bronze, which will rule over all the earth; and there will be a fourth kingdom, strong as iron. Just as iron crushes and subdues all things, so it will crush and subdue all things. And as you saw the feet and the toes partly of iron and partly of clay, it will be a divided kingdom, and some of the root of iron will be in it, just as you saw the iron mixed with the clay. And as the toes of the feet were partly of iron and partly of clay, part of the kingdom will be strong and part of it will be broken. As you saw the iron mixed with the clay, they will mingle with one another by the seed of men, but they will not hold together, one with another, just as iron does not mix with clay. In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, and his kingdom will not be left to another people. It will crush and winnow all the kingdoms, and it will itself stand for ever—just as you saw that a stone was cut from a mountain without hands and crushed the clay, the iron, the bronze, the silver and the gold. The great God has made known to the king what must come to pass after these things; and the dream is true, and its interpretation is sure."

When Nebuchadnezzar heard this, he remembered the dream and recognized that what Daniel had said would also come true; and he fell on his face and worshipped Daniel, and commanded that an offering and sweet incense be poured out to him. How great is the power of God's grace, beloved! The man who a little earlier was about to be put to death with the rest of the wise men of Babylon is the very one before whom the king falls down and worships, no longer as a man but as a god; and he commanded that an offering and sweet incense be poured out to him. Long ago, too, the Lord promised something similar to Moses, saying: "See, I have made you a god to Pharaoh," so that, through the signs he performed in Egypt, Moses might no longer be regarded as a man but be worshipped by the Egyptians as a god.

Astonished, then, at what Daniel had said, Nebuchadnezzar declared: "Truly your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords, and a revealer of mysteries, for you have been able to reveal this mystery." And the king made Daniel great and gave him many great gifts, and set him over the whole province of Babylon and made him chief of the satraps, over all the wise men of Babylon. Because Daniel had made himself small and declared himself the least of all men, the king exalted him and made him ruler of the whole province of Babylon. Pharaoh did the same for Joseph, when he made him ruler over all the land of Egypt. For in all Egypt no man was found able to declare the visions to Pharaoh except Joseph alone; and in Babylon none of the wise men could tell the king the vision except Daniel alone. For in every generation God draws holy men to himself, since he must be glorified throughout the whole world.

And Daniel made a request of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon. What Daniel did here also deserves trust and praise. For since they had joined Daniel in prayer to God that the vision might be revealed to him, Daniel too, when he had received rank and honour from the king, remembered them and laid before the king the part they had played, so that they too might be granted some honour as sharers in the mystery and godly men. For having asked heavenly things from the Lord, they also obtained earthly things from the king.

Now since blessed Daniel told the king the vision and did not keep silent about its interpretation, he left the inquiry to those with an upright mind, so that what Daniel said might in turn be interpreted by others. Lovers of truth must examine these things carefully, and not, reading them only in passing, suppose that what the prophets said was spoken to no clear purpose. He sees a great image, and states that its head is of fine gold; then he relates that its shoulders and chest are silver; then its belly and thighs bronze; then its legs iron; and likewise the toes of its feet clay and iron mixed together; then a stone cut from a mountain without hands, striking the image and crushing it; and the stone itself became a great mountain and filled the whole earth. Having said this about the image, he afterwards divides it according to its form and, applying it to kingdoms, explains it part by part. He says that the gold is King Nebuchadnezzar himself, declaring him to be the golden head of the image. Then he names a second kingdom, saying it is inferior: this is the silver. Then a third, which is the bronze. Then a fourth, strong, which is the iron. Then the extremities of the image's feet are shown to be clay and iron mixed together. For he began from the head, to show the gold; then the chest and the arms, and he names silver; then the belly and thighs, and he indicates the bronze; then he describes the legs, and points to iron; then the feet and the ten toes, and he declares clay and iron. After these nothing remains to be seen except a stone cut from a mountain and striking the image, becoming at the end a great mountain and filling the whole earth.

How then can we fail to understand what Daniel prophesied long ago in Babylon and what is still being fulfilled in the world now? For the image shown to Nebuchadnezzar at that time contained a figure of the kingdom of the whole world. In those times the Babylonians reigned, being the golden head of the image. Then after them the Persians held power for two hundred and forty-five years, so that they are shown to be the silver. After them the Greeks held power, beginning with Alexander the Macedonian, for three hundred years, so that they are the bronze. After them came the Romans, who are the iron legs of the image, being strong as iron. Then come the toes of the feet, to show the democracies that are to arise in various places, divided into the ten toes of the image, in which the iron will be mixed with the clay.

After this, what does Daniel say? "A stone was cut out without hands and struck the image." When the iron has been mixed with the clay and has reached the tips of the toes, and people have come to be at odds with one another, what remains to be awaited but Christ coming from heaven, like a stone cut from a mountain, to remove the kingdoms of this world and to set up the heavenly kingdom of the saints, which will never be destroyed, he himself becoming the mountain and city of the saints and filling the whole earth? That is why blessed Daniel said: "And after the end of those days the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, and his kingdom will not be left to another people." So that no one might doubt what had been said, wondering whether these things will really come to pass or not, the prophet set his seal on it, saying: "And the dream is true, and its interpretation is sure."

In the eighteenth year, King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden image, sixty cubits high and six cubits wide, and set it up on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon. And he sent to gather the high officials, the generals and the governors, the chiefs and the princes, and those in authority, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. And they all assembled and came, and stood before the image. And the herald cried aloud: "You are commanded, O peoples, tribes and languages: at the moment you hear the sound of the trumpet, pipe and lyre, sambuca and psaltery, and every kind of music, you are to fall down and worship the golden image; and whoever does not fall down and worship will at that very hour be thrown into the burning fiery furnace."

When a considerable time had passed and the eighteenth year had come, the king, remembering his dream, made a golden image, sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. For since blessed Daniel, in interpreting the dream, had answered the king, "You are the golden head of the image," King Nebuchadnezzar was puffed up by this word and, exalted in heart, made an image as a counterpart of that one, so that he might be worshipped by all as a god. Having made it great in size, he set it up on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon. And he sent and summoned the high officials, the generals, the governors and all those in authority to come to the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. Then, when all the people had gathered together and the instruments had sounded together, the peoples, tribes and languages fell down and worshipped the image—some of them out of fear of the king, but all becoming idolaters—and obeyed the word commanded by the king.

Then certain of the Chaldeans came forward and denounced the Jews to the king: "You, O king, have issued a decree that every person who hears the sound of the trumpet, pipe and lyre, sambuca, psaltery and bagpipe, and every kind of music, and does not fall down and worship the golden image, shall be thrown into the burning fiery furnace. But there are certain Jews whom you appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who have not obeyed your decree, O king; they do not serve your gods, and they do not worship the golden image that you set up." When the king heard this, in fury and rage he ordered them to be brought, and he said to them: "Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods and do not worship the golden image that I set up? Now then, if you are ready, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, pipe and lyre, sambuca and psaltery, and every kind of music, fall down and worship the golden image. But if not, at that very hour you will be thrown into the burning fiery furnace—and who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?"

You see the threat of a man, a tyrannical king, who did not know the one who said: "Do not fear people who can kill the body but cannot kill what is within; fear rather him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna." The youths, not cowed by these words, answered: "We have no need to answer you in this matter. For the God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will rescue us out of your hands, O king. But even if not, be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and we do not worship the golden image that you set up."

See: three youths who became an example to all faithful people. They did not fear the crowd of satraps, nor were they dismayed when they heard the king's words, nor did they cower when they saw the fire of the furnace blazing; instead they despised all people and the whole world, keeping only the fear of God before their eyes. Daniel, standing at a distance and keeping silent, taught them to take courage, smiling at them and himself rejoicing at their witness, as he saw three youths about to be crowned against the devil: not deceived by the art of music, nor enslaved by the pleasure of the instruments, nor led astray by the error of the Babylonians, nor submitting to the king's decree, nor bending the knee to a hammered golden image. These three were found faithful witnesses in Babylon, so that through them God might be glorified, Nebuchadnezzar put to shame, and the idols of the Babylonians shown to be nothing.

I will venture to say something, and I will run no risk in saying it: when these youths read the passage spoken by the prophet, they knew that it had been written about them. For how could the passage have said of Babylon, "I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to those who know me," unless it foresaw in the Spirit the mystery that was being worked out there? At that time, when they saw everyone worshipping the image and obeying the king's command, they set their minds on it and said: "This was not written idly, brothers; perhaps it will now be fulfilled in us. For look, the time has come. Our whole nation has been taken captive and made subject to the Babylonians. Nebuchadnezzar tyrannizes over us like a great devil, and he has made a golden image and is forcing us to commit idolatry. Let us remain faithful unto death. Let us not put our teacher Moses to shame, and let us not allow our nation to be laughed at. Let the three of us overcome the whole power of the Babylonians. God will deliver us from the king's hand, as he delivered our fathers from the hand of Pharaoh. Let us remember what happened long ago in the land of Egypt: how the sea was struck with the rod and was afraid; how the Jordan saw the ark and turned back; how Rahab the harlot was found faithful in the city of Jericho and was saved from the slaughter of the sword. Now too God is able to quench the fire of the furnace with ease. If he threatens us with the sword, let us endure death; if he threatens to throw us to wild beasts, let us not cower before the beasts. Let the crowd of Babylonians not overcome our faith." Encouraging one another like spirited athletes, they were led by the Spirit into the arena, three young boys contending against tens of thousands of unbelieving men.

But someone will say: "You are only speculating." Then learn, O man, what happened under Antiochus. The seven brothers were arrested together with their mother and were being beaten with whips and thongs. One of them answered and said: "What do you mean to ask and find out from us? We are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers." The king was enraged at this. He ordered pans and cauldrons to be heated at once, and he ordered the one who had been their spokesman to have his tongue cut out, to be scalped, and to have his hands and feet cut off while the rest of the brothers looked on. And as the vapour from the pan spread far and wide, they encouraged one another in their ancestral tongue, saying: "The Lord God is watching, and he truly has compassion on us, just as Moses made plain long ago in the song he spoke to the people's faces, when he said: 'And he will have compassion on his servants.'"

You see how the Spirit of the Father teaches the martyrs to prepare themselves. He urges and consoles them to despise this death and to hasten toward what is better. For if anyone is without the Holy Spirit, he is fearful and anxious. He hides in fear, dreads this passing death, cowers before the sword, and cannot endure punishment. He keeps this world before his eyes and worries about the things of this life. He puts his wife first, loves his own children, and seeks wealth and possessions. Such a person has not acquired heavenly power, and he easily perishes. So everyone who comes to the Word must listen to what the heavenly King and Master commands: "Whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me"; and "whoever does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple."

So it was then too: the three youths in Babylon, being disciples of the faith, answered the king and said: "We have no need to answer you concerning this matter." When Daniel heard these words, he approved. And again they said: "There is a God whom we serve, who is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will rescue us from your hands, O king." Blessed Daniel, since he was a prophet and foresaw the future, nodded that what they had said would truly come to pass. And to show the king how unsurpassable their faith was, the youths added: "But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and we do not worship the golden image that you have set up." When blessed Daniel heard this third saying from them, he marvelled at them and crowned them for their faith as noble athletes.

See how sure the words were that were spoken as with one mouth, so that they would not stumble in a single word. For when the king threatened them and said, "Why do you not serve my gods, and why do you not worship the golden image that I have set up?" they answered: "We have no need to answer you concerning this matter," for they did not consider him worthy of a defence on such a subject. Then, when the king said, "You will be thrown into the burning fiery furnace, and who is the god who will be able to rescue you from my hands?" they countered the word the king had spoken and said: "There is a God whom we serve, who is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will rescue us from your hands, O king." And when the king said again, "Now then, if you are ready, as soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, the pipe and the lyre, the harp and the psaltery, and every kind of music, fall down and worship the golden image," they said to him: "Let it be known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and we do not worship the golden image that you have set up."

For in one speech the king had put three statements before them, as though they were contending for three prizes, so that if he could ensnare them in even one statement he might trip them up. But they answered all three nobly, unwilling to be defeated in any of them. First, they treated the king's words with contempt, showing that the idol he worshipped was not worth any reply at all. Second, they taught the king whom one ought to fear and worship, saying: "There is a God whom we serve, who is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace." Then third, wishing to show their own faith, they said: "But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and we do not worship the golden image that you have set up." With this statement they made themselves secure. Otherwise, once they had been thrown into the furnace and burned up, the Chaldeans might boast and deceive the king, saying: "Do not be troubled, O king. You have won and taken the prize against them. For as they burned in the fire they cried out and said, 'We beg you, lord king, we will do what you command, we will worship the image.'" So that they might be called faithful martyrs even after death, they secured themselves in every way and refused to give the devil any opening. For they gave all the authority and the glory to God, believing that he is able to deliver us. "But if he does not will it, we would much rather die gladly than do what you have commanded."

Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with rage, and the look on his face changed toward Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, and he said: "Heat the furnace seven times over, until it is burning to the utmost." And he told mighty men of strength to bind them and throw them into the burning fiery furnace. Then those men were bound in their garments and their trousers [?] and were thrown into the burning fiery furnace, as the king had commanded. In truth, if the truth must be told, the youths prevailed [?]. For the more the youths' words prevailed, the more the king raged, and he said: "Heat the furnace seven times over," as though he had already been completely defeated by them. In earthly things the king prevailed, but in faith toward God the three youths prevailed. But someone will say: "Could Daniel not have pleaded for them, since he was the king's friend, and begged for the release of the three youths?" He could have. But he kept silent so that God's great works might be shown and the Babylonians might learn to fear God, and so that the youths' faith might be shown and God might be glorified in them. For if he had done this, the Babylonians would have said: "If Daniel had not pleaded with the king for them, they would have perished in the fire today." And it would have been thought a human favour rather than the power of God.

And why did the king, knowing that Daniel was a Jew, not take offence at all and say to him: "Why do you not worship the image?" Daniel would surely have told the king: "Because I do not revere things made by hands, but the living God, who made heaven and earth and has dominion over all flesh," just as he answered Cyrus in the matter of Bel. Carried away [?], the king said to him [?] ... Bel, except by the decision of the satraps: whoever makes a request of any god or man for thirty days, except of the king, will be thrown into the lions' den. But it was ordained that the three youths alone should be glorified in the furnace, and that Daniel alone should be thrown into the lions' den at the time of Bel, when Cyrus was king. So each of them was kept for his own appointed order and his own time, so that Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, seeing the three youths not harmed at all by the fire, might glorify God, and Cyrus the Persian, seeing Daniel not devoured by the lions, might be taught that the God of heaven alone is God. In this way God, ordering events at their proper times through his servants the prophets, persuades all people to come to the knowledge of him.

Then the youths were bound in their garments and their trousers and thrown into the burning fiery furnace, as the king had commanded. Tell me, Nebuchadnezzar, why do you order them to be thrown into the fire bound? So that they will not escape? Or so that, if they were untied, they would not stamp out the fire with their feet? But it is not you who are doing these things; there is another in you who is at work. That is why Scripture says: "Then the king's form was changed." For he was one thing and became another. At first the king was a man who feared God; then he exalted himself against God and was changed, imitating the works of the devil. That is why Scripture rightly declared beforehand: "I am God, and I do not change," to show that God is unchangeable and unalterable. The king's form was changed so that he might easily be understood to be a man, and so that the deceiver at work in him might readily be recognized, who always imitates the works of God and wants to deceive man in all sorts of ways. For, it says, "In the eighteenth year King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden image, sixty cubits high and six cubits wide, and he set it up in the plain of Deira in the province of Babylon." By the eighteen years he imitated Jesus, the Son of God, who, when he was present in the world, raised his own image, man, from the dead, and showed it to the disciples pure and spotless like gold. By the height of sixty cubits he imitated the sixty patriarchs, through whom the Word, the image of God, was formed and fashioned according to the flesh and was exalted above all the patriarchs. By the width of six cubits he indicated the six days of creation, for on the sixth day man was formed from the dust. So Nebuchadnezzar cast gold, made a counterfeit image, and set it up in the plain of Deira in the province of Babylon, signifying that the plain is the world and Babylon the great city. At that time Nebuchadnezzar made a single image, but now the deceiver has devised many more in the world, so that through many spectacles he may lead all people astray, carrying one here and another there: some worship the golden idol, others the silver, others the bronze, some the one made of ivory, and many revere the one of clay and of stone. All of them have abandoned the heavenly God and submitted to empty, lifeless and worthless idols. They refuse to look up on high or to contemplate the beauty of heaven, for fear that they might recognize its God and be able to be saved. These are the devil's tricks. He did not only work them long ago in Babylon; now too he does the same, and dares to attempt even worse against the servants of God.
