He has prepared a fiery furnace for himself so that through it he may terrify man, not knowing the eternal punishment by fire that God has prepared for him.

When these things had happened, Scripture says: "And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, fell bound into the middle of the furnace, and they walked about in the middle of the flame, singing hymns to God and blessing the Lord." The fire immediately consumed the bonds the king had put on them, but it did not touch their clothes or their trousers, so that in this too the greatness of God's work might be shown. For since the clothes were wrapped around the youths' bodies, they too were sanctified along with them and were not destroyed by the fire, but were honoured together with them through their witness. Let the heresiarchs who deny their own resurrection tell me how they can say that there is no resurrection of the flesh, when perishable clothes and shoes made from dead animals were not destroyed by the fire because they were wrapped around a holy body. How then will the flesh, perishable as it is, not be sanctified along with the holy soul it is wrapped around, and be transformed into incorruption? For if things that are perishable by nature did not suffer decay, how will that which was not made perishable by nature, but was put to death through disobedience, not rise again when it is brought back to life by the power of God? So in every way Scripture persuades us to believe in God with our whole heart, just as those youths believed and were brought safely out of the fiery furnace, whole, together with their clothes and trousers. For if the fire did not overpower them then, how can the eternal fire gain mastery over the saints who believe in God in the same way?

Then Azariah stood up with the others, and in the middle of the furnace they gave praise to God with hymn and prayer. First they recounted their own sins and those of their fathers, giving glory to God, acknowledging that they rightly and justly suffered these things as captives in a foreign land, handed over to a lawless king, the most wicked in all the earth, because their fathers had not kept the law of the Lord their God. Then, calling on the whole creation as though with one mouth, they sang hymns, glorified and blessed God, saying: "Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our fathers, and worthy to be praised and highly exalted forever." So, beginning with his holy, glorious and majestic name, they went on to the works of the Lord themselves, naming first the heavenly things, and they glorified him, saying: "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord; sing hymns to him and highly exalt him forever." Then they called on everything in order: the seven heavens, the authorities and powers in them, and the water above the heaven. They came to the firmament and named the lights in it, the sun, the moon and the stars, and said: "Bless the Lord, all you elements that move in the heaven; sing hymns to him and highly exalt him forever." Then they passed on to the changes of the air and the winds that are in the middle region of creation: winds, showers and snows, cold and heat, light and darkness, days and nights, and things like them. Then they came to the foundation of the earth. They began first with the glory of God itself and glorified it; then came the things above the heaven, those called supercosmic; then they named the firmament with its lights; then the things in the middle region of the firmament; then they turned to the earth, saying: "Let the earth bless the Lord; let it sing hymns to him and highly exalt him forever"; then mountains and hills; then everything that grows on the earth. Then they passed on to the waters, rivers, springs and seas; then the creatures that move in the waters, sea monsters and fish; then the birds of the air, cattle and wild beasts. Then they passed on to the children of men, offering up the hymn in due order. Then they named the beings below the earth, the spirits of the angels who keep Tartarus and the souls of the righteous, so that these too might sing hymns to God together with them. And when they had finished everything, they named themselves last, as the least and lowliest, saying: "Bless the Lord, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael; sing hymns to him and highly exalt him forever. For he has rescued us from Hades and saved us from the hand of death; he has delivered us from the midst of the burning flame, and from the midst of the fire he has delivered us. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever."

Tell me, three youths — and remember me, I beg you, so that I too may share with you the same lot of martyrdom — who was the fourth with you, walking about in the middle of the furnace and singing hymns to God with you as though with one mouth? Describe his appearance and his beauty to us, so that we too may recognize him when we see him in the flesh. Who was it who recounted the whole creation through your mouths in such good order, so that you left out nothing of all that exists and has come to be? You spent a single hour in the furnace and were taught how creation was made. For the Word was with you and speaking through you, he who also knows how creation was made. Indeed, beloved, what the three youths spoke in their hymns in the furnace is marvellous. See how they left out nothing that was created, so that nothing might be thought to be free or independent. Instead they embraced and named everything, things in heaven, things on earth and things under the earth, and showed that all are servants of God, who created all things through the Word, so that no created thing might boast of being unbegotten or without beginning. So let the teachers of the heresiarchs be silent, who name powers and aeons and emanations and invent empty fables. Through their strange words they easily deceive people and destroy them, and force them to worship things that do not exist as though they existed, fashioning other images in people's hearts, just as Nebuchadnezzar did. For Scripture embraces all things, whether principalities or authorities or powers or thrones or dominions or every name that is named, and has subjected them all and made them servants of God as their Lord and Master, to praise, bless and glorify their Maker. That is why Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, after naming everything that exists, added: "Bless the Lord, the God of gods, all you who worship him; sing hymns and give thanks to him, for his mercy endures forever."

When the Babylonians saw the three youths singing hymns in the furnace, they did not stop feeding it with naphtha and pitch, tow and brushwood, "and the flame streamed out above the furnace forty-nine cubits," for they too were fighting against God with all their might. "And the fire spread," it says, "and burned those of the Chaldeans whom it found around the furnace." Do you see how the fire itself is intelligent, recognizing and punishing the guilty? It did not touch the servants of God, but it burned up the unbelieving and godless Chaldeans. Those who were inside the furnace were refreshed with dew by the angel, while those who thought they were standing safely outside the furnace were destroyed by the fire. As Scripture says: "But the angel of God came down into the furnace together with Azariah and his companions, and drove the flame of the fire out of the furnace, and made the middle of the furnace like a whistling breeze full of dew. The fire did not touch them at all, nor did it hurt or trouble them."

We must ask, then: who was this angel who appeared in the furnace, keeping the youths safe in his arms as though they were his own children, turning the fire into dew for those inside and dealing out his judgment to those outside, as it is written, "With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you"? It was none other, unless I am mistaken, than the one who also judged the Egyptians in the water. For just as they had once thrown the male infants of the Hebrews into the river, so in the same way they perished in the sea, justly drowned in the water, so that an equal recompense might be paid to those who do evil. This was the one who received the authority of judgment from the Father, who also rained down fire and brimstone on Sodom and destroyed its people for their lawlessness and wicked impiety. Ezekiel too testifies that he took fire in his hand and holds it, waiting for the Father's voice, for when he will command him to cast it upon the world. When the fire in the furnace saw him, it was afraid; when it saw his surpassing light, it trembled. Of him Isaiah says: "And his name is called Angel of Great Counsel." Scripture also confessed him to be an angel of God, for it was he who announced to us the mysteries of the Father. He came down into the furnace together with Azariah and his companions. When the fire saw this angel, it recognized its own Master, and in fear it fled out of the furnace; and that is why it rose to forty-nine cubits. For it was driven from inside and gushed outward, and the middle of the furnace became a light, whistling dew, with no smell of fire inside at all. For the angel standing in the furnace was driving the flame from inside outward, and as it was driven out it streamed around the furnace to a height of forty-nine cubits.

Then Nebuchadnezzar, seeing what had happened, was amazed. He rose up in haste, heard them singing hymns, and said to his nobles, "Did we not throw three men, bound, into the midst of the fire?" They said, "Truly, O king." He answered and said, "But I see four men unbound, walking about in the midst of the fire, and there is no harm in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of God." Tell me, Nebuchadnezzar, when did you ever see the Son of God, that you should confess this one to be the Son of God? Who pierced your heart, that you should utter such a word? With what eyes were you able to look upon his light? And why was he shown to you alone and to none of the other satraps, unless it was because it is written, "The king's heart is in the hand of God"? This very hand of God, which was the Word, pierced his heart, so that he might recognize him in the furnace and glorify him. Nor is this point we have perceived an idle one. Since the children of Israel were going to see the Son of God in the world and not believe, Scripture showed beforehand that the Gentiles would recognize him in the flesh, whom long ago, when he was not yet in the flesh, Nebuchadnezzar saw and recognized in the furnace and confessed to be the Son of God.

Then Nebuchadnezzar came to the door of the burning furnace and said, "Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out and come here!" Since he himself could not go into the furnace, he called them to come out. He called the three by name, but for the fourth he could find no name to utter, for Jesus had not yet been born of the virgin. And the satraps, the generals, the governors and the king's officials gathered and looked at the men, and saw that the fire had had no power over their bodies, that not a hair of their heads had been singed, that their trousers were not changed, and that there was no smell of fire on them.

But perhaps someone will say: Why then did God rescue the martyrs of old, but not those of today? For we find that blessed Daniel was twice thrown into a den of lions and was not destroyed by the beasts, and that the three youths were thrown into the furnace and were not harmed by the fire. Take note, O man: even then God rescued those he wished still to live, so that God's mighty work might be displayed and proclaimed throughout the whole world to this day; but those he wished to be martyrs he crowned and took to himself. He rescued the three youths so that Nebuchadnezzar's boast might be shown to be nothing, since he wished to demonstrate that what is impossible with men is possible with God. For when Nebuchadnezzar said in his arrogance, "And who is the god who will be able to rescue you from the furnace of fire?" God showed him that he is able to rescue his own servants whenever he wills. The same thing happened in Daniel's case. When Darius said, "Has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to rescue you from the mouth of the lions?" Daniel answered and said, "God sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions, and they did me no harm." For the officers and the satraps had all contrived a pretext to kill Daniel by handing him over to the beasts; but God, knowing their wicked scheming and the simplicity of blessed Daniel, rescued him from the mouth of the lions. So he rescues whom he wills, and takes to himself whom he wills. For we also find the seven martyrs under Antiochus enduring terrible torments and being taken from the world. What then? Could God not have struck down King Antiochus and rescued the seven brothers? He could; but he did not will it, so that this might become an example for us. For if he rescued everyone, who would ever be a martyr? And if all were martyred and died, some unbelievers would say that this happens because God is powerless.

We must not, then, set ourselves against the will of God. "For whether we live, we live to the Lord; or whether we die, we die to the Lord; so whether we live or die, we are the Lord's." He rescued Jonah from the belly of the sea monster, because he willed it. He rescued Peter too from the hand of Herod, leading him out of prison, because he willed that he should still live; and in due time he took him, crucified for the Name, when he himself willed. He rescued Paul from many dangers, because he willed it; and after some time he took him, beheaded, and this too when he willed. He allowed Stephen to be stoned by the Jews, but because he endured, he crowned him. How would you be martyred today if they had not first been martyred and called blessed? So you have in the Old Testament many who were martyred and many who were rescued, so that the one and the same God might be shown to be God then and now, with authority to do with his servants whatever he wills. Let us come now to the King of glory himself and speak of the Son of God. Could God not have rescued his Christ, so that he would not be handed over to the Jews? Yes, he could; but he let him suffer, so that we might live through the death of his cross. And so the Lord, knowing God's will, said, "Father, not my will, but yours be done."

What is better for you, O man: to be martyred and depart this world in glory, or to be rescued and remain here to sin? For we know of many who confessed before the tribunal and, on some pretext, by God's providence, were released, and who then lived on for a considerable time and were found in transgressions. What did their confession of God profit them? It would have been better for them to depart this world pure, holding the heavenly crown, than to remain and heap up sins upon themselves, for which they must give an account. Therefore let anyone who is brought to trial for the sake of the Name pray to depart as a martyr, in whatever way it may be. For such a one is no longer even judged but will judge, having his own share in the first resurrection. Be steadfast, then, O man, never faltering in faith, and when you are called to martyrdom, answer readily, so that your faith may be made manifest. Perhaps God is testing you, as he tested Abraham when he asked for Isaac. If, once you have been brought to trial, he wills to rescue you, glorify God in this too. Imitate the three youths yourself, and consider their faith; for they said to the king, "God is able to deliver us; but if he does not will it, we are in God's power: we would gladly die rather than do what you have commanded." When Nebuchadnezzar then saw them come out of the furnace pure and unblemished, he was astounded and amazed; for not a hair of theirs was singed, nor were their trousers changed, and there was not even a smell of fire on them.

So Nebuchadnezzar answered and said, "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who sent his angel and rescued his servants, because they trusted in him; they defied the king's command and gave up their bodies rather than serve any god except their own God. And I issue a decree: any people, tribe or tongue that speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego shall be destroyed and their houses plundered; for there is no other god who can rescue like this." And he promoted Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the province of Babylon, exalted them, and appointed them to lead all the Jews who were in his kingdom. — We must observe, then, beloved, how great a grace faith in God bestows. For just as they glorified God himself by handing themselves over to death, so in turn they themselves were glorified not only by God but also by the king, and they taught foreign and barbarian nations to worship God. Indeed, one can truly see this happening even now. Whenever one of the saints is called to martyrdom and God works some mighty deeds for him, all who see it immediately marvel, and many come to believe through them and so become martyrs of God themselves. Believing in him, let us too present ourselves worthy to God, keeping ourselves pure in body, soul and spirit, so that we too may receive the crown of incorruption and, together with the blessed martyrs, sing hymns to God. For to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Nebuchadnezzar the king, to all peoples, tribes and tongues that dwell in all the earth: may your peace be multiplied. It has seemed good to me to make known to you the signs and wonders that God has worked with me, for they are great and mighty. His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion is from generation to generation. I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and flourishing. I saw a dream, and it frightened me; I was troubled on my bed, and the visions of my head alarmed me. And I issued a decree to bring before me all the wise men of Babylon, so that they might make known to me the interpretation of the dream. And the magi, the Gazarenes and the Chaldeans came in, and I told the dream before them, but they did not make its interpretation known to me, until Daniel came, whose name is Belteshazzar after the name of my god, and who has the holy spirit of God in him. To him I said: "Belteshazzar, chief of the enchanters, since I know that the holy spirit of God is in you and that no mystery is too hard for you, hear the dream that I saw, and tell me its interpretation."

Nebuchadnezzar, then, having seen the wonders that had befallen the three youths and being struck with amazement, published them openly by decree to all the peoples, tribes and tongues under his rule, so that they too, hearing what had happened, might fear God and glorify him, just as he himself said in praise: "His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion is from generation to generation." Then he related what happened concerning his second vision: how none of the magi, Gazarenes or Chaldeans could declare the matter to the king, until Daniel was summoned, the one who had also explained his first vision to him. This was so that in everything God might glorify his own servants the prophets above the other barbarian and foreign nations, who thought to exalt themselves in their own human wisdom, being trained in earthly learning. For the grace and gift that come from God are from above, from heaven, and bestow their own riches on those who are worthy; and the blessed prophets shared in this grace, being continually given understanding by the Holy Spirit. As the apostle also says, writing to the Corinthians: "And I came to you, proclaiming to you the mystery of Christ, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people." So too in Babylon the earthly wisdom of all the wise men was made foolish, since they could not interpret the king's dream, until Daniel came, who had the holy spirit of God in him. To this the king himself bore witness, having tested him in many things, and he set it forth publicly in writing, so that Daniel might appear honored not only by the king himself but might also be named by all the king's subjects as a man of God and a great prophet. Just as the Egyptians long ago, having seen the wonderful works done through Moses in the ten plagues, were afraid and named him Mennouthim, which in Egyptian means "man of God" (for "mennou" means man and "thim" means God), so Nebuchadnezzar also bore witness concerning Daniel that he had the holy spirit of God in him.

When Daniel had then been summoned and stood before the king, the king answered him: "On my bed I was looking, and behold, a tree in the middle of the earth, and its height was great. The tree grew great and strong, and its height reached to heaven and its breadth to the end of all the earth. Its leaves were beautiful and its fruit abundant, and in it was food for all. Under it the wild beasts made their dwelling, and in its branches lived the birds of the sky, and from it all flesh was fed. I was looking in the vision of the night on my bed, and behold, a Watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven and cried aloud and said: 'Cut down the tree and strip off its branches, shake off its leaves and scatter its fruit. Let the beasts be driven from beneath it and the birds from its branches. But leave the stump of its roots in the earth, and in a band of bronze and iron, and in the grass outside and in the dew of heaven he shall lie down, and his portion shall be with the beasts in the grass of the earth. His heart shall be changed from that of men, and the heart of a beast shall be given to him, and seven times shall pass over him. The matter is by the decree of the Watcher, and the inquiry is the word of the holy ones, so that the living may know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and will give it to whomever he pleases, and will set over it the lowliest of men.' This is the dream that I, King Nebuchadnezzar, saw; and you, Belteshazzar, tell me its interpretation, for all the wise men of my kingdom cannot make its interpretation plain to me, but you, Daniel, can, because the holy spirit is in you."

Now the dream seen by Nebuchadnezzar was shown to the king himself as a rebuke. Because his heart was lifted up and he exalted himself against God, setting up a golden image and compelling everyone to be idolaters, it was shown to him by a vision that he too was under the authority of God, even though he then thought he reigned above all kings. And to show that the kingdom had been given to him by God, Daniel said to him: "You, O king, are king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given a kingdom strong, mighty and honored in every place where the sons of men dwell." And Nebuchadnezzar himself, marveling when Daniel interpreted the dream, likewise said: "Truly your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, since you were able to reveal this mystery." Since, then, forgetting his former words, he afterward exalted himself in pride, he received this rebuke from God and became an example and a pattern for all people, tyrants and kings alike, so that they should not think thoughts beyond what is human and be boastful, nor exalt themselves against God and glory in it, but should rather foresee their own danger and fear God, knowing that they too have a Lord in heaven. For Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, who became king of Syria, after tormenting the servants of God with various tortures and daring the worst crimes, afterward himself met with the punishment he deserved from God, being struck by a divine scourge, so that he could not even bear his own stench, but while the impious man was still alive worms swarmed out of his eyes. For this reason, though he resorted to many supplications and confessions to God, he did not obtain salvation from him. Despairing of himself, and coming at last to a recognition of human limits, he said as he was about to die: "It is right to be subject to God, and that one who is mortal should not think himself equal to God." So all the kings who conducted themselves reverently and in a God-loving way were honored by God, while all who were puffed up beyond what is fitting in their own conceit received from God a fitting and just punishment in return. In the same way Sennacherib, who boasted in his own great power and reproached God with lying words, was struck by the angel, losing one hundred and eighty-five thousand men in a single night; and afterward he himself was slain by his own sons in his own land, according to the word of the Lord which he spoke through Isaiah the prophet, so that all people might recognize the heavenly authority.

The same thing happened to Nebuchadnezzar. For he set up the image at the beginning of the eighteenth year, as was said in the preceding book, where its dimensions were also given; and when the year was completed, after twelve months, the kingdom was taken away from him, so that the dream he had seen might be fulfilled, and the one who had carried others into captivity might himself become a fugitive in the mountains, and the one who had punished the Hebrews in a foreign land might himself be justly punished in a desert land. As Scripture relates, saying: "Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was stunned for about an hour, and his thoughts troubled him. And Belteshazzar answered and said: 'My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you, and its interpretation for your enemies. The tree that you saw, which grew great and strong, whose height reached to heaven and its breadth to all the earth, whose leaves were flourishing and its fruit abundant, and in which was food for all, under which the wild beasts dwelt and in whose branches the birds of the sky made their nests—it is you, O king, for you have grown great and strong, and your greatness has increased and reached to heaven, and your dominion to the ends of the earth. And whereas the king saw a Watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven, who said, "Uproot the tree and destroy it, but leave the stump of its roots in the earth, and in a band of bronze and iron, and in the grass outside and in the dew of heaven he shall lodge, and his portion shall be with the wild beasts, until seven times pass over him"—this is its interpretation, O king, and it is the decree of the Most High which has come upon my lord the king: they will drive you away from men, and your dwelling shall be with the wild beasts; they will feed you grass like an ox, and you shall lodge in the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and will give it to whomever he pleases. And whereas he said, "Leave the stump of the tree's roots," your kingdom will remain yours from the time you recognize the heavenly authority. Therefore, O king, let my counsel be pleasing to you: redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; perhaps there will be forbearance toward your offenses.' All this came upon King Nebuchadnezzar. After twelve months, as he was walking in the palace of his kingdom in Babylon, the king spoke and said: 'Is not this great Babylon, which I have built as a royal residence by the might of my power, for the honor of my glory?' While the word was still in the king's mouth, a voice came from heaven: 'To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: your kingdom has passed from you, and they will drive you away from men, and your dwelling shall be with the wild beasts; they will feed you grass like an ox, and seven times shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and will give it to whomever he pleases.' In that very hour the word was fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: he was driven away from men and ate grass like an ox, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven, until his hair grew long like a lion's and his nails became like birds' claws. And at the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and praised and glorified him who lives forever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion and his kingdom is from generation to generation, and all who dwell on the earth are counted as nothing, and he does according to his will in the host of heaven and among those who dwell on the earth, and there is no one who can withstand his hand and say to him, 'What have you done?'"

The dream, then, seems to interpret itself and to be quite plain to all, just as Scripture teaches that these things happened in this way, and the king himself afterward, in his confession, related what had befallen him. Yet the grace of God generously gives understanding to people, so that, keeping our minds unhindered in all things, we may not fix our attention on the persons of human kings—for vain is hope placed in man—nor flatter rulers appointed to positions of authority for the sake of a gift, but may devote ourselves to God alone and do what is pleasing to him, and so both pass the present life free from danger and easily escape the judgment to come. For what can a king or a ruler profit a person, when he himself, being mortal, moves under the authority of the one who made him? He can indeed bestow on you many great gifts in this present life, but these too are earthly and temporary. Many who have received honor and gifts from a king and been appointed to certain offices have afterward been brought into danger through their own doing, either being found to be conspirators, or being put to death by others as friends of the king. What did their friendship with the king profit them, who neither had their fill of the gifts they received, and lost their own lives besides? Flee, then, from such persons, O man, lest you be brought into danger because of them. For all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass: the grass withers and the flower falls. Hear what was said by the apostle Paul, how he exhorts Timothy, writing: "Charge the rich of this present age not to be haughty, nor to trust in the uncertainty of riches, but to hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe."

For if the glory of those who hold high positions is like dry leaves, which flourish for a little while and then quickly wither, what did King Nebuchadnezzar gain by his arrogant words when he said, "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built as a royal residence by the might of my power, for the honor of my glory?"—seeing that he was driven out and ate grass with the beasts in the mountains? Where was that boldness, and the great pride of his words, and the great and terrible flame of the furnace, when he was not even master of his own soul? And for this reason the blessed Daniel became his counselor, wishing, like a good physician, to heal his wounds, saying: "Now let my counsel be pleasing to you, O king: redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; perhaps he will be forbearing toward your offenses." That is why, as he interpreted the king's dream, he was grieved even to tears and was stunned for about an hour, and his thoughts troubled him, and he did not wish to utter a sound from his mouth. In this he showed the affection he had for the king, so that by this the king too might be pierced with compunction and, by doing what the prophet said, be able to be saved. So while Daniel stood speechless for an hour and a deep silence had fallen, everyone saw him troubled by his thoughts and his face changing: at one moment turning pale from fear of the interpretation, lest the king, on hearing what was said about him, become enraged and order him to be put to death; at another moment strengthened by the Spirit and taking on the face of an angel, his countenance becoming fiery and his eyes shining like a flame of fire, so that by this too the king might be struck with awe and be afraid. For if the children of Israel could not look upon the face of the blessed Moses because of the glory of his face, how could the Babylonians then not have been afraid when they saw Daniel's face transformed? At one moment he appeared to be a man, and at another he was shown to be like an angel of God. And they all stood speechless, waiting for the thoughts that would come forth from his heart. Then, calmed from the great glory and anguish and returning to the normal state of his human nature, he answered the king and said: "O king, may the dream be for those who hate you, and its interpretation for your enemies." And beginning in this way he declared to him point by point what was going to happen to him, and comforting him with words of consolation he restored him to good hope for what was to come. For he says to him: "And whereas the king saw a Watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven, who said, 'Cut down the tree, strip off its leaves and shake off its branches, but leave the stump of the tree's roots in the earth'—your kingdom will remain yours, O king, until you recognize the heavenly authority, that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and will give it to whomever he wishes."

All these things, then, happened to King Nebuchadnezzar after twelve months. For neither did Scripture lie, nor did Daniel deceive him; rather, he taught him beforehand the things that were going to be fulfilled upon him. For by the tree that grew great and strong, whose height reached to heaven and its breadth to the end of all the earth, Scripture signifies the king himself, as Daniel also explicitly made clear, because the king was exalted and became glorious and ruled over all the earth and held sway over far-off nations. [Its branches were the consuls, generals, governors and all who had been appointed by him, put forth like branches from a tree.] The leaves of the tree indicate the decrees issued by his word, which he sent out into all the earth, commanding and ordaining as he wished. [The abundant fruit that the tree bore signifies the great revenue and the tributes brought to him from each and every nation. Its breadth, set firm upon the earth, signifies the kingdom itself, because it is earthly, being established as it were upon the earth.] Its abundant fruit, and the food for all that was in it, are the wages, the honors and the gifts given by the king to all, which were like food given to people from a tree. The wild beasts that dwelt beneath it are meant to be the armies and the forces, which always remained in attendance on the king and waited on him, carrying out his commands, being like wild beasts, ready to make war and destroy and to tear people apart like beasts. The birds dwelling in its branches are the obedience of all the nations to him, which, coming from far and distant places, were subject to the rulers appointed by him, as to branches from a tree.

Now the angel's coming down from heaven and saying, "Cut down the tree and shake off its branches, strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit; let the beasts be driven from beneath it and the birds from its branches," signifies the conspiracy that arose against the king among the satraps and the forces under him. Driven out by them, he fled into the desert, and his kingdom was taken from him, along with the authority and greatness he had formerly possessed. And the one who once boasted and said, "Who is the God who will deliver you out of my hands?" afterward [bent pitiably toward the ground] lived among the beasts in the mountains, roaring, afraid of his own satraps lest he be killed by them. And for this reason Scripture says: "In the grass outside and in the dew of heaven he shall lie down, and his portion shall be with the wild beasts in the grass of the earth. His heart shall be changed from that of men, and the heart of a beast shall be given to him." For the great king and ruler no longer lived as a man, dwelling in palaces, but living alone in desert places he ate grass and herbage, until his heart was changed and became like that of a beast grazing in the woods and caves, until his hair grew like a lion's and his nails grew long like birds' claws, and seven times passed over him. For it was God Most High who decreed that these things should happen thus, as Daniel says: "It is the decree of the Most High which has come upon my lord the king." And the Word, having heard the Father's counsel, came down from heaven and announced the Father's will to the angels, as Scripture says: "A holy one came down from heaven." And the angels asked the Word: "What has the Master commanded us to do?" For "the inquiry is of the holy ones." And the Word said to them: "Thus says God Most High: Cut down the tree, strip off its branches and shake off its leaves." And when they heard this, they stirred up the king's forces so as to take his kingdom away from him. For all the nations have been entrusted to angels, as John says in the Revelation: "And I heard one saying, 'Release the four angels who are seated at the great river Euphrates'"—these were the angels of the Persians, the Medes, the Assyrians and the Babylonians.

Then it says: "And in the grass outside and in the dew of heaven he shall lodge, and seven times shall pass over him, until he knows that God Most High rules over the kingdom of men." Now some reckon the seven times as seven years; others take them as seven seasons, each changing every three months—for the year has four seasons: winter, spring, summer and autumn—so that seven seasons then passed over the king. And his saying, "Leave the stump of the tree's roots in the earth," shows that he was to be restored again to his own rule according to the will of God. For this happened to the king for his correction, so that, no longer proud, he might be able to say from then on: "And he is able to humble all who walk in pride."

We find in the records that Nebuchadnezzar reigned for twenty-five years. He reigned for the first eighteen years, when in his pride he set up the image. Then, twelve months later, this befell him: he was driven away from among men and the kingdom was taken from him. But when he had been humbled and had prayed to the Lord, confessed, and made supplication to God the Most High, his nobles sought him out, and he returned and reigned again for seven years. He himself tells of this, saying: “At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High and praised and glorified him who lives for ever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion and his kingdom endures from generation to generation. All who dwell on the earth are counted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and there is no one who can stay his hand or say to him, ‘What have you done?’ At that same time my reason returned to me, and I came back to the honour of my kingdom; my form returned to me, and my lords and my nobles sought me out, and I was established over my kingdom, and still greater majesty was added to me. Now therefore I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and glorify the King of heaven, for all his works are true and his ways are justice, and he is able to humble all who walk in pride.” When he had laid aside the great pride he had acquired, and, in anguish among the mountains, had made confession to God and acknowledged the heavenly power, he was restored once more to the rule of his kingdom. His nobles and lords and all who were under him sought him out, and they even bestowed on him greater honour and glory, so that what had been said in the vision might be fulfilled: “But leave the stump of its roots in the earth, until he knows that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will.”

Such, then, were the things that befell King Nebuchadnezzar in those times, and they were written down for the admonition and remembrance of all people, just as Daniel recounted them in the forms and visions, as things that truly took place. When we come to that passage, we shall compare the two and show that they agree and are true. For Nebuchadnezzar saw two dreams: that of the image of many materials, and then that of the tree. Daniel interpreted them, and they will also be fulfilled in their own time. In the same way Daniel sees four beasts coming up out of the sea, of which some things have already happened and others are yet to come. We do this so as to show that Daniel's prophecy agrees with and is equal to the rest, differing in nothing, as proof of things that have already happened, that now are, and that are still to be. For if we believe that the things already fulfilled have proved true, how will not all that is to come also prove true, the things the blessed prophets announced beforehand as going to be? Everything will be fulfilled according to the counsel of God, advancing in its own appointed times.

Let us see, then, what Scripture says: “King Belshazzar made a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, and the wine was set before them. And as Belshazzar drank, he commanded, while tasting the wine, that the vessels of gold and silver be brought which Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple in Jerusalem, so that the king and his nobles, his concubines and his wives might drink from them. ‹So the vessels of gold and silver were brought which Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple of God in Jerusalem, and the king and his nobles, his concubines and his wives drank from them.› They drank wine and praised the gods of gold and silver, of bronze and iron, of wood and stone. In that very hour the fingers of a man's hand came forth and wrote opposite the lampstand on the plaster of the wall of the king's palace, and the king watched the knuckles of the hand as it wrote. Then the king's countenance changed, and his thoughts troubled him; the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees knocked together. The king cried aloud to bring in the magicians, the Chaldeans and the soothsayers, and he said to the wise men of Babylon, ‘Whoever reads this writing and makes known to me its interpretation shall be clothed in purple, with the chain of gold about his neck, and shall rule as third in my kingdom.’ Then all the king's wise men came in, but they could not read the writing or make known its interpretation to the king. And Belshazzar was troubled, and his countenance changed, and his nobles were thrown into confusion.”

After the death of Nebuchadnezzar, then, his son Evil-Merodach succeeded to his kingdom. Scripture makes no mention of him, either because he lived piously or because nothing remarkable happened in his time. He reigned twelve years, and after him his brother Belshazzar, about whom Scripture now gives its account. In the fourth year of his reign he made a great feast for a thousand of his nobles. While they were at their drinking, the king, puffed up with pride, ordered the vessels of gold and silver that Nebuchadnezzar his father had brought from the temple in Jerusalem to be brought in, so that his nobles and his concubines might drink from them. Things that other kings had dedicated to God for his glory and honour they took up in their defiled hands, poured libations from them, and praised lifeless and immovable idols. When this was done, “the fingers of a man's hand came forth and wrote opposite the lampstand on the plaster of the wall of the king's palace.” In the case of Nebuchadnezzar it was said, “A holy one came down from heaven”; here it says, “the fingers of a hand came forth,” Scripture signifying that the Word himself was to become embodied in the last times and take on the form of a man, so that he would no longer be seen as in a vision, but, having become man in the flesh and lived among men, would accomplish the will of the Father. By writing the writing on the wall, then, Scripture signified that he was the very one who had engraved the law of God on the tablets on the mountain, as Scripture says: “And the tablets were written with the finger of God, and the writing was the writing of God engraved on the tablets.” So here too the fingers of the hand were shown to the king alone, flashing opposite the lampstand, so that what was written there might be recognized as the writing of God. For the light of the hand, shining against the light of the lamp, dimmed its light, so that the fingers writing on the wall might be seen.

When the king saw them, he became terrified and was seized with great trembling, and “cried aloud to bring in the magicians, the Chaldeans and the soothsayers,” not understanding that it was not given to these to read the writing of God, but to those who from childhood had been trained in the law of God and had come to know the divine writings from their fathers. When they had all been summoned, the king said to them: “Whoever reads this writing and makes known to me its interpretation shall be clothed in purple, with the chain of gold about his neck, and shall rule as third in my kingdom. And all the king's wise men came, but they could not read the writing or make known its interpretation to the king.” How many of the Babylonians at that time contrived in many ways, hoping to invent some strange saying to please the king, so as to be clothed in purple and honoured on the third throne! But the word was hidden from them. Their eyes were dimmed and the thoughts of their hearts were blinded, for “the Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.” So when all of them declined, the king's heart was troubled and his countenance changed, and his nobles were thrown into confusion. Then the queen, hearing what had happened, came into the banqueting hall and said to the king: “Do not let your thoughts trouble you, nor let your countenance change. There is a man in your kingdom in whom is the spirit of God, and in the days of your father watchfulness and understanding were found in him. King Nebuchadnezzar your father appointed him chief of the enchanters, magicians, Chaldeans and soothsayers, because an excellent spirit of God was in him, and wisdom and understanding, interpreting dreams, declaring hidden things and solving riddles — Daniel, to whom the king gave the name Belteshazzar. Now let him be called, and he will declare the interpretation to you.”

What, then, was the reason for the queen coming in and mentioning Daniel? Did not all the nobles and friends of the king know him? Or did they not know what had happened in Nebuchadnezzar's time — that he alone had interpreted the king's dreams, and that the king had made him chief over the wise men of Babylon? They knew it well enough themselves, but because they envied him, since he was adorned with heavenly wisdom, they did not want to tell the king about him, lest he should come and read the writing and they themselves be put to shame afterwards. And this did not happen only to Daniel then; it still happens to many even now. For whenever someone, having proved worthy, obtains grace from God and is found wiser than others, at once everyone looks askance at him, and they hate him, persecute him, insult him, dishonour him, slander him and despise him, so that by this they themselves may seem to be something when they are nothing. The same thing happened to the prophets, to the Lord, and to the apostles. So too we shall understand what befell Daniel in Babylon, for as Scripture proceeds it will show that these things happened in this way.

Then the king, having heard about him, ordered Daniel to be brought in and said to him: “Are you Daniel, one of the exiles of Judah whom Nebuchadnezzar my father brought here? I have heard of you, that you are able to give interpretations. Now if you can read this writing and make known to me its interpretation, you shall be clothed in purple, the chain of gold shall be about your neck, and you shall rule as third in my kingdom.” But blessed Daniel, taking no delight in earthly gifts and not elated by royal honour, answered: “Let your gifts be for yourself, O king, and give the rewards of your house to another; yet I will read the writing and make known its interpretation to you.” And so, beginning from the start, he related to the king in order everything that had happened to his father, at once instructing him about what had taken place and teaching him not to be boastful or proud beyond what is fitting, since he was under the power of God. So he said to him: “The Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father the kingdom and majesty, honour and glory. And because of the majesty he gave him, all peoples, tribes and tongues trembled and feared before him. Whom he would he killed, and whom he would he struck down; whom he would he raised up, and whom he would he brought low. But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit hardened in pride, he was brought down from his royal throne and his honour was taken from him. He was driven away from among men, his heart was made like the beasts', and his dwelling was with the wild asses; they fed him grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, until he knew that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will.” Having said this, he added what follows, at the same time rebuking the king and showing him no partiality, so that on hearing it he might be afraid and at once recognize the sin he had committed. So he says: “And you, his son Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart before God, though you knew all this, but you have lifted yourself up against the Lord, the God of heaven. You have had the vessels of his house brought before you, and you and your nobles, your ‹concubines and your› wives have drunk wine from them; and you have praised the gods of gold and silver, of bronze and iron, of wood and stone, which do not see or hear or know; but the God in whose hand is your breath, and all your ways, you have not glorified. Therefore the knuckles of a hand were sent from his presence, and this writing was inscribed: MENE, TEKEL, PERES. This is the interpretation of the matter: MENE, God has numbered your kingdom and brought it to an end; TEKEL, it has been weighed in the balance and found wanting; PERES, your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.”

When the king heard the writing and its interpretation, he was grieved at what had been said, but he ordered Daniel to be clothed in purple and to be third ruler in the kingdom. “That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was slain, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being sixty-two years old.” Once the interpretation had been given by Daniel, as Scripture records, that very night ‹the word was fulfilled and the kingdom of the Babylonians passed› to the Medes, as Daniel had said: “He sets up kings and removes them; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light is with him.”

So Darius, also called Ahasuerus, received the kingdom and “appointed a hundred and twenty satraps, and over them three officers, of whom Daniel was one, to whom the satraps were to give account, so that the king might not be troubled. And Daniel was above them, because an excellent spirit was in him, and the king set him over his whole kingdom.” For Darius the Mede, having heard about him — about the wisdom he possessed and his faithfulness and piety from childhood — appointed him first among all his friends and lord over his whole kingdom, just as Pharaoh did when he granted Joseph the honour of second place to his own royal throne and made all the rulers of Egypt subject to him. When this was done, the officers and satraps, moved by envy, sought to find a pretext against Daniel, so that, seizing on some occasion against him, they might accuse him and put him to death. Thus the saying we spoke a little earlier was fulfilled: whenever someone is devout and fears God, having grace and wisdom from God, he is hated by other men, because they themselves were not counted worthy of the same grace. So too the satraps and officers hated Daniel out of envy, since he was wiser and more trustworthy than all. Scripture bore witness to this, saying: “And they found no pretext, no fault and no error against him, because he was faithful.” For he not only kept God's commandments according to the law, but also managed the king's affairs with great care and exactness, unwilling to stain his own clean conscience in any sordid matter for the sake of a little gain.

How many at that time pretended to be Daniel's friends while hating him in their hearts! They sent him gifts secretly through other people and promised to give him large sums of money, wanting to test his integrity, so that, having then got a pretext against him, they might go to the king and accuse him of giving away the king's possessions, and so have him put to death as a traitor. They were always seeking, by every device, a charge against him; and when they found none, they at last took counsel together, saying: “We shall find no pretext against Daniel except in the law of his God.” Then, being of one mind, they came to the king and said: “King Darius, live for ever! The governors and satraps, the consuls and prefects of your kingdom have taken counsel together to establish a royal statute and enforce a decree, that whoever makes a request of any god or man for thirty days, except of you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions. Now therefore, O king, establish the decree and sign the writing, so that it cannot be changed, according to the law of the Persians and Medes.” Then Darius, unaware of the wicked purpose they had devised, ordered the decree to be written and publicly posted. Indeed, later on Haman too, wishing to kill Mordecai and his people, went to King Artaxerxes and gave similar counsel, that by royal decree all the Jews should be killed on a single day, the fourteenth of the twelfth month.

When Daniel learned of what had been written, he understood the plot that had been laid against him, yet he was neither afraid nor dismayed, being ready rather to be given as food to the beasts than to submit to the king's command. He also had something to spur him on: what had happened to the three young men, how, refusing to worship the king's image, they were saved from the furnace of fire. And so, going into his house, he opened the windows in his upper room facing Jerusalem, and three times a day he knelt down on his knees and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done before.

We should take note, then, of the piety of blessed Daniel: though he seemed fully occupied with the affairs of state, he nevertheless persevered in prayer day by day, rendering to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's. But perhaps someone will say: “What then? Could he not have prayed to God in his heart during the day, and at night devoted himself to prayer in secret in his house as he wished, so as not to run into danger?” He could have, but he would not. For if he had done so, the officers and satraps could have said: “How does he fear God, when he has feared the king's decree and submitted to his commands?” And they would have brought some reproach and charge of unbelief against him, for that would have been the act of hypocrisy, not of fear of and faith in God. That is why he gave his adversaries no occasion for slander; for to whatever a person submits, to that he is also enslaved.

Those who believe in God ought neither to play the hypocrite nor to fear those set in authority, unless they do something evil. But if, because of their faith in God, they are compelled to do something contrary to it, they should gladly die rather than do what is commanded. For when the apostle said that we should be subject to all the governing authorities, he did not mean that we should deny our faith and the things God has commanded and do whatever men order, but that, fearing the authorities, we should do nothing evil, so that we are not punished by them as evildoers. That is why he says: “He is God's servant, an avenger on those who do evil. What then? Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it. But if you do evil, be afraid, for it does not bear the sword in vain.” So he told us to be subject in this sense: to live holily and devoutly in the present life, keeping before our eyes the danger of the sword. The apostles, when forbidden by the rulers and scribes to speak the word, did not stop, obeying God rather than men; and for this reason, in their anger, they put them in the public prison. But the angel led them out by night and said: “Go and speak the words of this life.”

In the same way Daniel, when forbidden to pray, did not submit to the king's decree, so as not to place the glory of God below the glory of men. For if someone dies for God's sake, he ought to rejoice in this, having found eternal life. Those who labour well [?], then, living purely and in fear in this world, must give no occasion to those who seek an occasion, so that by this the seekers themselves may rather be put to shame — just as the officers then sought to find an occasion against Daniel and found none, because he was faithful. But if some try to force us not to worship God or make requests of him, threatening us with death, it is far sweeter to die than to do what they command. “For who shall separate us from the love of God? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or peril, or sword?” And so blessed Daniel, fearing God rather, and giving himself up to death, was saved from the lions by the angel. For if, out of regard for the decree, he had kept quiet for those thirty days, his faith toward God would no longer ‹have been› pure: “for no one can serve two masters.” The devil's craft has always been of this kind: to persecute, afflict and wear down the saints, so that they may not lift up holy hands to God in prayer, for he knows that the prayer of the saints brings peace to the world but punishment to the evil one. So it was in the wilderness: whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered them, Amalek prevailed. This still happens even now and is fulfilled in us. For whenever we cease praying, the adversary prevails against us; but when we persevere in prayer, the power and authority of the evil one are brought to nothing.

In the same way, then, he was at work at that time in the officials and satraps, to accomplish his own will through them and to have the blessed Daniel thrown into the lions' den. They watched him, and when they saw him praying three times a day they went to the king and said: "King Darius, did you not issue a decree that anyone who makes a petition of any god or man for thirty days, except of you, O king, shall be thrown into the lions' den?" He said: "The word is true, and the decree of the Medes and Persians shall not pass away." They said to him: "Look, Daniel, one of the sons of the captivity of Judah, has not submitted to your decree, and three times a day he makes his petitions to his God." When the king heard this, he was greatly grieved over it and strove to deliver Daniel. For he saw through their scheme: because they hated Daniel, since he was wiser and more distinguished than all of them, they had devised this plot against him, wanting to hand him over to the beasts by treachery. So he argued with the satraps to see whether he could beg him off and save him from the danger. But so that Daniel would not be rescued by a man, and it be thought a king's favour, but would rather be seen as a work of God accomplished in him, when it was already evening and the king was still pleading with the satraps on his behalf, they said: "Know, O king, that it is a decree of the Medes and Persians that no ordinance or statute that the king establishes may be changed." With this argument they wanted to shame the king into giving way, implying that if the decree he had laid down were not made binding and firm, everything else he decreed would also be thought invalid.

For what reason, then, did the satraps accuse Daniel alone? For surely the three young men were also praying with him; if they had not obeyed Nebuchadnezzar's command, still less would they obey Darius's decree. The reason is this: just as back in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, although Daniel was present, the Chaldeans accused no one but the three young men, because the martyrdom was reserved for them, so now in the time of Darius they accused Daniel alone, for the calling was his. For in every season God does not lack a man through whom he may be glorified, as the prophet says: "He who makes his array will call them one by one by name."

So then, since Darius could no longer argue against the satraps, he ordered Daniel to be brought, and they threw him into the lions' den. And the king answered and said to him: "Your God, whom you serve continually, will himself deliver you," urging him to take heart, as if to say: "Since I wished to and could not, even though I am king, the God whom you serve will himself deliver you"—so that what is impossible with men might be shown to be possible with God. And they brought a stone and laid it on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his signet ring, so that nothing might be changed in Daniel's case. This too was an act of malice: the satraps, afraid that the king might secretly order him to be drawn up out of the den, asked for the stone to be sealed—just as the rulers of the Pharisees did in the case of the Saviour, sealing the stone and posting the guard.

When this had been done, the king went away to his house and went to bed without supper; no food was brought to him, and sleep left him. — How much a righteous man who fears God can accomplish, that the king, grieving over him, would not even take food! The satraps spent the whole night rejoicing, as though they had won a prize against Daniel, but the king lay awake all night mourning, having unjustly lost such a man, and fearing that he himself might come into danger because of him. For he was well aware of what had befallen Nebuchadnezzar and what had happened in the time of Belshazzar: the one was driven from his kingdom, the other was slain that very night because of the holy vessels. Then he rose early at first light and went in haste to the lions' den, and calling out with a loud voice he said: "Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the mouth of the lions?" What moved the king to utter these words, if not that he had heard what had befallen the young men, who refused to submit to the king's command and were saved from the fiery furnace? [?] the same thing would happen in Daniel's case, since he had feared God and treated the decree of the Medes and Persians as nothing.

And Daniel said to the king: "My God sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions, and they did not harm me, because uprightness was found in me before him; and before you too, O king, I have committed no offence." — How much it means to put one's confidence in God rather than in men! For men give up hope and hand over to death, but God does not forsake his servants. That is why the psalmist teaches, saying: "It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man; it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes." Then, when the angel appeared in the den, the wild beasts were tamed, and the lions wagged their tails and fawned on him with joy, submitting to him as to a new Adam. They licked Daniel's holy feet and rolled about in his footprints, longing to be trodden underfoot by him themselves. For if we believe that when Paul was condemned to the beasts, the lion let loose on him lay down at his feet and licked him all over, how shall we not also believe what happened in Daniel's case, which Darius himself recounted to everyone by sending out letters? And these things are in fact recorded to this day in the books of the Persians and Medes, so that not only the Hebrews, nor only the Babylonians, but also the Medes and Persians and all the nations dwelling under heaven might hear what happened and themselves fear God. So too at that time Darius, hearing Daniel's voice, was struck with amazement and marvelled. He ordered the stone to be rolled away and saw Daniel sitting in the midst of the lions, stroking their manes with his own hands. Then he called everyone together and showed them the astonishing sight: wild beasts tamed by a man and fondled in his hands. When Daniel was brought up out of the den, no injury of any kind was found on him, because he had believed in his God.

Then the king gave the order, and they brought the men who had slandered Daniel, and they were thrown into the lions' den, they and their sons and their wives; and they had not reached the floor of the den before the lions overpowered them and crushed all their bones. So those who trust in a human king and dig a pit for their neighbour will themselves fall into it and perish. So it happened then also in the case of the three young men: the fire did not overpower those who were in the furnace, but it burst out and burned up the Chaldeans outside. For the eyes of God justly assign to people the judgement they deserve. So it happened also to Haman in the meantime, who wanted to destroy Mordecai and his race in a single day: he prepared a gallows fifty cubits high for him, and was hanged on it himself along with his whole household. Now those who accused Daniel and handed him over as food for the beasts were themselves destroyed by the lions.

Then Darius wrote to all the peoples, tribes, and tongues dwelling in all the earth, proclaiming peace to all, and by the decree he then issued compelling them to revere God, as it says: "From my presence a decree has been laid down in every dominion of my kingdom, that people should tremble and fear before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall not be destroyed, and his dominion is to the end. He helps and rescues, and works wonders and signs in heaven and on earth; he has delivered Daniel from the hand of the lions." Consider this: today Babylon is the world, its satraps are the powers, Darius is their king, the den is Hades, and the lions are the angels of punishment. So imitate the blessed Daniel: do not fear the satraps or submit to a human decree, so that, when you are thrown into the lions' den, you may be guarded by the angel, tame the beasts, and be bowed down to by them as a servant of God; that no corruption may be found in you, but you may be brought up alive out of the den, be found a sharer in the resurrection, gain mastery over your enemies, and give thanks to the ever-living God. — For to him belong the glory and the power to the unending ages of ages. Amen.

"In the first year of Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, Daniel saw a dream, and the visions of his head as he lay on his bed, and he wrote down the dream." Whatever the Spirit revealed to the blessed prophet in visions, he recounted freely to others as well. He did not want to seem to be prophesying the future only for himself. He wanted to show himself a prophet for others too, for all who wish to search the divine Scriptures with faith. So he says: "I, Daniel, was watching, and behold, the four winds of heaven were stirring up the great sea, and four great beasts came up out of the sea, each different from the others. The first was like a lioness and had wings like an eagle's. I watched until its wings were plucked off; it was lifted up from the ground and set on its feet like a human being, and a human heart was given to it. And behold, a second beast, like a bear; it was raised up on one side, and it had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth, and it was told: 'Arise, devour much flesh.' After this I watched, and behold, another beast, like a leopard, with four wings of a bird on its back; the beast had four heads, and authority was given to it. After this I watched, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and dreadful and exceedingly strong. Its teeth were of iron and its claws of bronze; it devoured and crushed, and it trampled what was left with its feet. It was exceedingly different from all the beasts before it, and it had ten horns. While I was considering its horns, behold, another horn, a little one, came up among them, and three of the earlier horns were uprooted before it. And behold, in this horn were eyes like human eyes, and a mouth speaking great things. I watched until thrones were set in place and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was a flame of fire, and its wheels were burning fire. A river of fire streamed out before him. A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court sat, and books were opened. Then I watched because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking, until the beast was slain and destroyed and its body was given over to be burned with fire. As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, but they were granted a prolonging of life for a season."

Different beasts were shown to the blessed prophet Daniel, each unlike the others. We must therefore understand that he is not talking about actual beasts. He is showing, in figure and image, the kingdoms that have risen up in this world and that destroy humankind like wild beasts. By "the great sea" he means the whole world, and the "four winds of heaven" signify creation with its four corners. So when he says, "I saw four beasts coming up out of the sea," he means the kingdoms of this world. "The first was like a lioness and had wings like an eagle's." By "lioness" he names the kingdom of the Babylonians, which Nebuchadnezzar then ruled. He says "it had wings like an eagle's" because the king was exalted. He was puffed up in his heart and lifted himself up against God, because he had become great and glorious. Then he says: "Its wings were plucked off; it was lifted up from the ground and set on its feet like a human being, and a human heart was given to it." This really did happen to Nebuchadnezzar, as is recorded in the preceding book, and he himself bears witness that it happened to him: he was driven out of his kingdom, and the glory and greatness he had once possessed were taken from him. Any bird whose wings are plucked becomes helpless and easy to catch. In the same way the king's forces deserted him then, the very forces in which he had seemed to boast and grow proud. He was afraid of them and fled into the wilderness so as not to be killed by them. When the prophet says, "It was set on its feet like a human being, and a human heart was given to it," he means this: Nebuchadnezzar humbled himself and recognized that he was a man, subject to God's authority. He prayed to the Lord, obtained his compassion, and was restored once more to his kingdom and glory. He himself testifies to this when he says: "At the end of those days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me. I blessed the Most High, and I praised and glorified the one who lives for ever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom endures from generation to generation. All the inhabitants of the earth are counted as nothing, and they are as nothing."

These things happened to Nebuchadnezzar in those times, just as the blessed Daniel has shown us in the vision, and as the king himself confessed. Then his dynasty came to an end under Belshazzar, when Belshazzar was slain in the night because of the deed he had committed, as the preceding book records, and Darius the Mede, aged sixty-two, took over the kingdom. So the prophet fittingly describes another beast coming up, the bear, to signify by it the kingdom of the Persians. "And three ribs," he says, "were in its mouth." By the three ribs he means three regions of nations over which this beast ruled: the Medes, the Assyrians and the Babylonians. "And it was told: 'Arise, devour much flesh.'" For in those times the Persians rose up, laid waste the whole land, enslaved many people and destroyed them. The bear is a filthy, flesh-eating animal that tears with its claws and teeth, and the kingdom of the Persians proved to be just like it. They held power for two hundred and thirty years. (Some historians, however, have recorded that they ruled for two hundred and forty-five years, down to the reign of Darius. Alexander of Macedon overthrew him in the seventh year and transferred the kingdom of the Persians to Greece.) As Daniel also says: "After this I watched, and behold, another beast, like a leopard, with four wings of a bird on its back; the beast had four heads, and authority was given to it." By naming a leopard he signified the kingdom of the Greeks, whom Alexander of Macedon ruled. He compared them to a leopard because they were quick of mind, full of schemes in their reasoning, and bitter of heart. The animal likewise has a spotted, many-colored appearance and is quick to do harm and to drink human blood. "With four wings of a bird on its back," he says, "and the beast had four heads." For after Alexander's kingdom had been exalted, had grown, and had become famous throughout the whole world, it was divided into four realms. When Alexander was dying, he divided it among four men who had been brought up with him and were of his own people: Seleucus, Demetrius, Ptolemy and Philip. All of these put on crowns, just as Daniel foretells and as is recorded in the first book of Maccabees.

After the Greeks had held power for three hundred years, the prophet again points out something further to me. For he says: "After this I watched, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and dreadful and exceedingly strong. Its teeth were of iron and its claws of bronze; it devoured and crushed, and it trampled what was left with its feet. It was exceedingly different from all the beasts before it, and it had ten horns. While I was considering its horns, behold, another horn, a little one, came up among them, and three of the earlier horns were uprooted before it. And behold, in this horn were eyes like human eyes, and a mouth speaking great things. I watched until thrones were set in place and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was a flame of fire, and its wheels were burning fire. A river of fire streamed out before him. A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court sat, and books were opened. Then I watched because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking, until the beast was slain and destroyed and its body was given over to be burned with fire. As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, but they were granted a prolonging of life for a season."

It is plain to everyone that after the kingdom of the Greeks no other kingdom has arisen except the one that rules now and still stands. It has teeth of iron because, like iron, it subdues and crushes everyone by its own strength. "It trampled what was left with its feet" because no other kingdom will remain after it. Instead, ten horns will spring up out of this very kingdom, and among them a little one will come up and uproot three of the first ones. In the case of the leopard, the prophet foretold that the beast had four heads, and it happened: Alexander's kingdom was divided into four realms. In the same way we must now wait until ten horns arise out of this very kingdom. That will happen when the beast's time is fulfilled. Then the little horn, which is the Antichrist, will suddenly appear among them, righteousness will be taken away from the earth, and the whole world will come to its end. So we must not try to run ahead of God's purpose. We must be patient and pray that we may not fall into such times. Nor, on the other hand, should we disbelieve, as though these things were not going to happen. If the earlier things the prophets foretold did not take place, then do not expect these either. But if those took place at their appointed times, just as had been foretold, then these too will certainly be fulfilled. When people say, "And when will these things happen?" they speak as unbelievers, not as believers. But to know beforehand what is to come and to believe that it will happen so is the mark of a blessed man, one who knows and keeps silent, so that he may not put himself in danger by saying too much.

Let us show in another way that these things are true and have been made plain to the servants of God. Scripture tells no lies at all, and the Holy Spirit does not lead astray his servants the prophets, through whom it pleased him to announce God's purpose to humankind. He did this so that when we see these things happening we may not stumble, nor be thrown into confusion as though we were seeing something strange. For the end cannot come upon this world in any other way than this. In the days of Sodom, as soon as their transgressions had reached full measure, fire came down on them at once and they perished. So it will be now. When lawlessness has multiplied in the world, and the beast that is now made of iron has been divided into the ten horns, and there are upheavals and discord, with different men in different places tearing the realm apart, then the end will come upon them.

We have already dealt with these matters in another treatise. There we did not pass over the coming of the Antichrist and his descent, where the deceiver will come from and how, and what he will do. Even so, I will now recall these things briefly, so that a person may stand firm in every respect, without wavering in mind in anything, and so be able to believe God with his whole heart. When the blessed Daniel interpreted the vision for Nebuchadnezzar (I mean the vision of the image), he declared that its head was gold, then its hands, arms and chest silver, then its belly and thighs bronze, then its legs iron, and then its feet, in which part was iron and part clay. By this he meant to show what he has now set out in his own vision through the beasts. The gold is the kingdom of the Babylonians, which was the lioness. The silver is that of the Persians, which was the bear. Then the bronze is that of the Greeks, whom Alexander of Macedon ruled, and so it points to the leopard. After these he speaks of legs of iron, to signify the terrifying and dreadful beast with iron teeth. This is the Romans who now hold power, strong as iron. After the iron legs of the image, what remains but the feet? They have ten toes, a mixture of clay and iron. The ten toes signify the ten horns, and the clay and iron signify their discord: they will be mixed together with the seed of men, but they will not hold together, one with another. Just as iron does not mix with clay, so at that time people will not be able to agree with one another. Different men will be carried off in different directions in disorder, and they will divide the realm among themselves by nations.

The grace of God richly instructs those who have set their hope on him and have despised this world. So we will not pass over this question either: why did the blessed prophet name all the kingdoms that came before by likening them to beasts, but not say what kind of beast the kingdom that now exists would be? I will speak about this more clearly, so that what is said may be better understood.
